THE PILOT OF THE MERRY JANE.
BY J. MACLAREN COBBAN, Author of "The Angel of the Covenant," "The King of Andaman," "The Red Sultan," Sze.

It was a wild night, and threatened to be wilder. The wind raged and bellowed up the narrow, steep streets of the old town, and banged and buffeted at doors and windows.; the sea persistently roared like a vast menagerie of hungry wild beasts, and the rain lashed everything as with whips of steel. That was just as it grew dark. When the night was quite set in, the storm, as if taking advantage of the secrecy of darkness, let its fury go. It raged, it ramped, it , foamed, and it screamed without intermisAion. Those who were indoors, on the houses on the cliff, could not hear each other speak, even behind double windows; and those who ventured into the streets were enveloped, drenched, whipped, and stung by a bitter, salt, and ferocious something:, which was neither rain nor. sea-spray, but a com- pound of both, mixed with sand. But few ventured far, for the lower streets were also filled with billows of driven foam, like the suds of a vast and terrific washing. The harbour, which was just under the northern nose of the bay, was a very difficult port to make in such a nor'easter as was abroad; and so, besides the steady white light of the small lighthouse at the pier-head, there burnt high in the storm-brazier (which was almost of the height of the lighthouse) a great fire of blazin,. coal. A little beyond that pier ran the breakwater, like a protecting arm, so that all the brazier experienced of the wild, wet weather on the sea was a ggan ti c hissing handful of spray now and then trom the waves that beat upon and leaped the breakwater. To keep the brazier-fire burning there was a man —the people of the little town called him "a creature "—who was named Thomson. No one, not even Thomson himself, knew whence he had got the name. But he accepted it, and was everywhere known by it—as a dog might be called "Jack" or "Towzer. " He had no Christian name. He was of no account. He was nobody's child; he was the "creature "of the town. The town in one way and another fed and clothed him, and the town shewed its proprietary rights in him by cuffing and kicking him on occasion, but for the most part by chaffing and teasing him. The town had tried keeping him in the workhouse ; but restriction of his freedom made Thomson a raging and foaming wild beast. With the fullest liberty he was abso- lutely harmless and tolerably useful, so complete liberty was allowed him.

He' was a giant, with a giant's strength. His clothing was of the lightest and scantiest; he pre- ferred it _so, and yet he never seemed to be cold. And he always chose to be barefoot—which was considerate to the town, for no ordinary human shoe would have contained his foot, huge and soft as the pad of a camel. Well, to and fro at the pier-end Thomson paced all that night, for he never slept in a storm; the disturbance of the elements seemed to disturb and keep awake his poor wits. Backward and forward he swung on his great, soft pads, giving a constant eye to the brazier, and now and then lowering it to add coal, and ever muttering thickly to himself, or bellowing forth over the boiling, hissing waters, with his hand to his mouth: "Port, you lubber! Port Hard-a-port !" These were his favourite words, and so well recognised were they as his that he would often be saluted or hailed in the street with "Port, Thomson! Hard-a-port !" whereupon he would look in wonder and smile, like a shy child. So the storm raged and screamed and roared, and Thomson roared back and swung to and fro and kept the brazier burning all the night long. In the morning at the first show of light the harbour-master came forth from his den by the lighthouse. The storm had abated a good deal with the turn of the tide, and the rain had ceased. As the day grew, ancient mariners and fishermen in great boots and with their hands thrust deep into flap-eared pockets came rolling down the pier. As the storm had subsided, so had 'Thomson. He sat down in a corner with his back against the wall and his head looking out between his knees. It

div.p: was tne naroour-master tnat trampen to anti fro, when the mariners, with pipes or quids, rolled to the pier-end. "It bain't half-done," said an old salt, after eyeing the scurrying rack of clouds and the angry gleam of sun flashing out in the south-east. "It wur a stiff night," said the harbour-master, stopping in his walk and laying a firm emphasis on the words, as to imply that, in his opinion, the night could not very well have been "stiffer." "It wur nou't, harbour-master," said the old fellow, squirting the juice of his quid over the edge of the pier, "nou't to the gale in Feberwary wur fifteen year. Thoo minds on't, Jim," turning to another old man. "There wur ten sail ashore atwixt the fish-pier there and the mussel-beds, and a Dutch Galliot wur druv clean slap into block- yard. Bah! Last night wur nou't, harbour- master!"

"Well, Sam'l," said the harbour-master, "we dean't want it wuss, nor so bad." He resumed his tramping; but presently he stopped again to say: "We dean't want to skeer company wloam again as is coming in for t'winter, and company would be skeerecl wi' another day and night like t'last." "Ah !" came in a breezy murmur of anxiety from all the mariners and fishermen, for the town was of the seaside sort that lays itself out to attract "company." Of course there was always a consider- able number of visitors in the summer; but the "company" most desired were the invalid and well-to-do people who spent money pretty freely, and who shewed a‘growing disposition to come for the winter.

"Aye," said Sam'l, "a good dale o' company in t' town. Company's a fine titling for t' town— company is. Gi'es mair empl'yment—company does; a good price for fish an' all. And fair fond o' sailing in cobles—company is.,, "Yiss, Sam'l," said the harbour-master, planting himself square before the old man, "company's a splendid thing for t' town, if town can keep t' company—if t' town can keep 'em. Mark my words," he added, looking round, "this winter'll be the making o' t' town—if we can keep it oop - came from all in a subdued and anxious murmur.
"Two yawls driving round from the nor'ard 1" cried a man who stood with a spyglass in a look- out perch which gave him a view clear over the breakwater.

The harbour-master was at once on the alert. "Are they oor own, Jack?" he called. Jack peered through his glass a second or two. " Yiss," he answered. "No. 39 and No. 64." "That's luck for them," said the harbour-master, grimly. "If they warn't oor own never a blessed stick or stitch on 'em should come in 'ere."

"Of coorse not, harbour-master," said old Swill, with a grin. "Let 'em go ashore. I'm short o' firewood for t'winter, mysen!" They all laughed; they understood the joke, for these worthy mariners and fishermen had no objec- tion to be wreckers on occasion. -

,"Ah, but," said the harbour-master, "(lon't ye go for to misunderstand my meaning. If ou't come ashore this bout, ye'd best leave it alone, or ye may get smnmat more nor ye bargain for." "What, maister ?" asked one, taking his pipe from his mouth and looking. "What, thoo numskull ? " said the harbour- master. "Dos'tna know that every port up and down •but our own rots wi' small-pox? If we should get it in here, in yawl or schooner, barque or brig, the Lord help us and our hopes o' company Company would be off on t' wing like a school -' crows at even ! "

"Quarantine 'em," said the man. "Quarantine 'em ? " cried the harbour-master. "I'll quarantine 'em! Oh, yiss, I'll quarantine 'em! Thoo can tak' thy davy o' that The rest nodded in grim assent. For a genera- tion ago people had a fear and horror of small-pox which people to-day have not, because they have never seen its ravages. "Now look," broke out the harbour-master, with _ _

a rough laugh, "look at that blessed idiot, Thomson! Seems as if he understood every word I said. But, of course, he dean't. We'll quarantine 'em, wean't we, Thomson ? " "Port " cried Thomson, lifting up his head. "Hard-a-port!" " Port! Hard-a-port ' " cried the harbour- • master, mocking him. "The blessed idiot is like a parrot or cockytoo I Never a sensible, Christian word, but only 'Port! Hard-a-port ! ' Wed, t' Almighty should be easy on• him at t' Judgment Day ! ' The yawls sighted by Jack presently shot close round the end of the breakwater and the lighthouse pier. at the same instant arm-minr their sails

(according to the cuitom of all who knew the peculiarities of the little harbour), with intent to 'Ede alongside the pier and inward with Ihe way on them. But the terrific swirl in the bay and into the harbour made a strong underflow of water out; and the yawls would have been carried away and driven ashore, had not a dozen deft and ready hands thrown ropes, and so hauled the boats in. By noon the tide turned again. The gale began to renew its strength and fury, and the rain again flew on the wings of the wind, and stung the skin like needles. Before one o'clock there came another lull. The wind blew as if a little tired of it,: furious exertion ; the rain ceased, and the clouds drew up from the sea and put on an appearance of shape. It was then that the story of the town's shame begins.

well out ana- flit o the nor ara. ne accoinplishez. that not a moment too soon, for, just as she turned to run again for the harbour the storm, Like a monstrous winged thing, came flying again out of the nor'east, hissing and screaming over the glooming, whitening waters. With a defiant bellow at the storm Thomson pushed the skipper from the wheel, and seized it himself. It was no moment for hesitation or quarrel. The skipper, in his superstition about idiots and his shrewd observation of the masterly way in which Thomson handled the wheel, let go, and stood by. With a firm grip, and with even something like intelligence in his eye, Thomson held the wheel; and the schooner, like a race-horse feeling the rein, sped forward madly for the breakwater, as if she would leap it. An enormous sea swept her up well-nigh to the height of the lighthouse. It seemed as if she would either ..sweep over the 'breakwater, or be dashed on it. But. the sweeping, scouring water swept rather round than over the breakwater. "Port ! Hard-a-port I ,roared Thomson to him- self and to the storm. _ • _
"A sail to nor'ard !" cried the man with the spy- glass on the look-out perch at the end of the pier. "A schooner !--flying distress-signal 1"

"Ah ! " said the harbour-master, clambering up on the perch to look with his own glass. There was a schooner or two belonging to the port: it might be one of them. More probably it was not. It it was not—then! The harbour-master resolutely gripped his jaws. "She sails weel," said the look-out man; "lifts hersen weel out o't' water. What can be wrong?" ...

Instantly, with a giant's might, he turned the wheel and shoved it Clown hard on the port side, as the schooner cleared the end of the breakwater pier, and, like a creature instinct with life, obedient to her helm, turned her nose for the lighthouse pier. - - "A-ha! Ha!" roared • Thomson, waving a freer hand towards the one sail that.was,up, and making a, motion downward. . _ _ _

"Topsails, gone," said another mariner who-had clambered up on the perch. "That's nou't to fly signals about!" said the harbour-master, fiercely. He watched the schooner as she bore down. Seeing how wide she kept of the breakwater end, when she should have shoved her helm hard-a-port if she meant to run in, "She's a stranger," he cried, "or she'd know the trick of making the harbour." Still he watched her, and he saw she had only to be let alone to drive away to the south'ard and go to pieces on the mussel-beds; it would be impossible for her to tack enough into the wind to make the harbour now. The harbour-master saw that at once, and a gleam of satisfaction shone in his eye. Meanwhile a crowd of "company" was, on the cliff-top watching the ship with tender sympathy and ignorant wonder; lont.,not one of them guessed that the harbour-master was wittingly allowing the ship to drive to destruction and imperilling his own immortal soul for their precious sakes. The schooner was still driving, when down came her foresail and her mainsail and sha ceased to drift. _

"Down sail !" roared the skipper, while he him- self ran with his one able assistant to lower the big jib. With an effective way on her, the schooner swept towards the harbour, and .shot along the inner side of the lighthouse pier. .There was by that time a tolerable company of mariners and others gathered at the pier-end, who had. become acquainted with the fears .of the harbour-master, and made them their own. The schooner had accomplished a most daring and successful feat, and they looked through Elle flying spray to see who had been the ruler of it. To their amazement: they saw at the wheel the despised and derided Thomson. He had brought the schooner in; he had brought the dread pes- tilence ; a shipload of seeds of disease under their nose—he, the despised idiot! They opened their mouths in inadness, and roared curses at him. They pressed forward tc shake their fists at him. Meanwhile the schoonez was losing her way. The fierce underflow which swept round and out of the little harbour was seis- inv her keel in its relentless grip. "For God's sake, cried the skipper, "throw a !" _ _ . .
"Curse her!" roared the harbour-master. "She's anchored!" _

In a minute or two he was on board a pilot-boat, with the powerful Thomson pulling a couple of oars —that was one thing that the gigantic idiot could do—and in a few minutes more the boat was sweep- ing within a few yards of the schooner. "Ship ahoy t" roared the harbour-master. "Merry Jane, of Sunderland," replied a big man in oil-skins, looking over the ship's side, "in ballast from Dover."

But no hand threw a line from the pier; and wiry eye looked only hatred of the idiot, or dread of the pestilence that was believed to be on Doan, the ship. "You cannot come in here, skipper I " bellowet' the harbour-master.

The skipper desperately tried to cast a lint: ashore himself, thinking that, if those on the pie: were men at all, they would not refuse to make it fast. But the fierce nor'easter caught the coils o' the line and flung it bad; and the ship was lost Away she drifted; and speedily she drove to hey doom on the sunken roe4ks on the south of the bay. The skipper clambered along to the wheel where, Thomson stood monumental, his head diand armt and feet bare and his poor rags clinging drenched' to his body.

"Thoo cannot 'come in, skipper," said the harbour-master. "'Tis almost low water, and this is a horrible bad harbour to make wi' a stiff nor'-easter. Thoo'dst best run to the south'ard. Thoo'll get round the Nab whilst t' lull lasts, and make Flixenby right enough." "All right. You may stow your advice, 'master. 'Tis a doctor I want. Ye should ha' plenty of doctors in a place like this." "A doctor ? " cried the harbour-master.
"Aye, a doctor. Get me a doctor, like a good man. I'll pay him weel," said the skipper. "I've two lads and my own lass down wi' summat." "What?" cracked out the harbour-master.

"My poor lad," cried the skipper, "this is nc fault o' yourn ! You ha' done well! But may God forgive those villains on the pier!" Through a terrible welter of wind and sea, raft and spray, the schooner drove to destruction. Foi a quarter of an hour or so—which seemed half s life-time—she and those on her deck battled witb the storm, striving to head her for the sandy part of the shore, but all in vain. A harsh scraping and grinding, the lift of a great sea, a bounce that shook her from stem to stern, aml the skipper knew that the end had come.

"The Lord knows," said the skipper, "I don't." By that time the boat was scraping the schooner's side, and Thomson was keeping the boat in place by clinging to a rope's end. "Fall away ! " cried the harbour-master. But—for what reason Heaven alone knows— Thomson swung himself out of the boat and on board the schooner with the quickness and ease of a cat.

" 'Tis all up I" he cried. "We must commit us to God's mercy, for men ain't got none! Can ye swim, my poor lad ? " he roared to Thomson. For answer Thomson bellowed "Port! Hard-a- port I " and swung off to the cabin. He slid in a second down the companion stairs, the skipper after him 'in his heavy boots. While the skipper rid himself of these encumbrances, he was astonished by seeing the idiot go to the bunk where the fair-haired girl lay tossing in her fever. With wonderful care and tenderness he wrapp id her about with the bedclothes, and took her in hi:: arms. With an instinct of trust in the simp e giant she put her arms about his neck, and lay content, while an extraordinary smile of joy illumined the face of the idiot. The skipper saw the whole incident with open-mouthed astonish- ment, and before he could say, a word, Thomson was gone with the child up the companion stairs again. The skipper followed in all haste, but only an time to see Thomson with the child swept shore- ward on a great wave. What followed it is impossible to describe. But in less than half-an-hour some men, hurrying along the cliffs to the rescue, found the girl in a niche oi the cliff out of reach of the sea and still wrapped in her bedclothes. At first they thought she was dead; but soon they were convinced she was but sleeping softly. A little further off they found the skipper—alive, but terribly bruised, and ignorant of his daughter's fate. But Thomson—poor Thomson !—was not found till next day, when his body drifted ashore away to the south, battered by the sea out of all knowledge. You may guess how the men from the pier felt when they looked in silence on the bruised and sodden corpse of the heroic idiot; and what shame crept into their hearts later when they. knew that the sickness of the child, of which they had beer in so panic a fear, had been nothing but a touch of fever, from which the drenching of the sea ha,i miraculously- recovered her. [Tin: END. 3

"Come back, Thomson!" cried the harbour- master. "Come out o' that, thoo idiot! If thoo dean't come out o' that this minute, thoo'll never come ashore again I" But Thomson only roared in answer his catch- phrase: "Port, ye lubbers ! Hard-a-port ! " The skipper looked hard at. his visitor anoi shrewdly guessed what he was. Moreover, the ship's dog had made instant friends with Thomson, and Thomsoewith him.
"He's a poor idiot, eh?" said the skipper, pity- ingly-. "Well, harbour-master, he can bide till you send the doctor."

The pilot-boat fell away, while the harbour- master swore, and was rowed back to the pier with one pair of oars. On board the schooner the skipper was surprised with the conduct of Thomson. As if he were thoroughly acquainted with the ship; he passed directly to the cabin, and there found the bunk in which a pretty fair-haired girl, the daughter of the skipper, lay tossing. It touched the father's heart to see the poor idiot stroke her hair and her cheek while he thickly murmured "Bonny ! • Bonny!" and while he moaned and whined like a faithful and affectionate dog. Moreover, it struck the skipper with wonder to note that the idiot's action and voice seemed to have a soothing effect upon the sick child.

----- Like many a sailor, he was superstitious about those whom God has afflicted; and so when Thomson suddenly swung up on deck again and began hauling on the main sheet, he and his one active sailor aided the idiot. _ _ _ _

"And what next, Thomson ? " said he, looking wistfully at the uncouth giant. For answer Thomson gurgled and grinned, and went through a pantomime of running forward on the deck and then doubling back and making a sharp circle to his right. "Ah, what?" said the skipper. "The Lord help ! What does the poor soul mean ? " Thomson seemed to perceive ,he was not under- stood. He pointed out to sea, made an inward semi-circular sweep of his hand, and roared: "Port ! Hard-a-port !" "Oh, au," said the .uncomprehending skipper. "Now, if ye only had your wits, Thomson, and could tell us what might be your meaning." "Seems to me, skipper," said the sailor, "that the looney wants to p'int out, so to speak, how you should make the harbour."
"Lord!" cried the skipper. "That's it. Happen, the poor idiot, by the mercy o' God, has come to save us !"
The lull in the storm still continued while the schooner tacked out. The skipper was at the wheel and Thomson stood swaying on the other side of it readx,to lend .a. nlTh.e schooner had tacked

_ He seemed about to I)tir,t out into a paroxysm of rage, but I remained si!elit, looking him steadily .n the face. He hesitated, faltered, and turned away his eyes. Not a word passed between us, but he knew what I had seen! We walked home ir perfect silence. From that hour Douglas was more subdued. He tried to keep up the affectation of boisterous cheer- fulness but he no longer carried conviction. From time to time I caught him scanning my face with a sort of suppressed anxiety, as though he feared to read in/my eyes that I had once more beheld the spectre. A struggle was evidently going on in his mind between pride and fear. I thought oncc• or twice ,of suggesting that, we should both returr to ETeidelburg. Alas! I did not do it. The last day came. It was a beautiful summer afternoon. Douglas was sitting on a bench in the garden, resting after a game of lawn-tennis' in. which he had sliewn irritation over his own bad play. I was standing some distance oft with my racquet still in my hand, and then, all at once, I was aware, for the third time, of the presence of the spectre of Scale. Had it risen out of the ground like a miasma of the marsh? Was it something more than a mere illusion of the eyesight, something different from the incorporeal spii;its who wander between earth and heaven? I thought of the terrible Sein-Lacca of Scandinavian legends, the phosphoric emanation of the grave. I thought again of that horrid creature of Etruscan superstition, the half-demon, half-human Larva that emerges from decaying tombs to prey upon the living. To such a monster I compared the ghastly thing before me, with its hideous mask of more than mortal hatred, stepping with the movement of a loathsome scorpion towards its unconscious victim. ,

Just as the Form stopped beside him, Douglas looked, and caught my stare of terror. "For God's sake, Forbes, speak out! What do you see? " he cried out in a kind of hoarse scream. "I see It—the spectre!" I gasped back. "Where! Oh, my God! Where is it ? " he almost shrieked, rolling his eyes round. "There! Close beside you. Look, it is going to touch,you again!"

Even as rriy lips shaped the words the frightful fingers extended themselves till they came in contact with the blackening scar. Douglas looked up. His eyeballs distended them- selves. An awful change passed into them. He saw what touched him.

In the same moment the spectre was gone, like a reflection from a mirror when the object which casts it is removed; and then—then I beheld what I would cut off my hand never to have witnessed. For where I had seen those fingers touch the man's forehead there burst out a most appalling green stain of the bi.aness of a man's palm, and as I rushed forward, the whole of that side of the forehead, where the scar had been, rotted away like soft cheese, and became putrid before my eyes, with a stench that turned me sick.
It is understood that the last laird of Scale died of cancer of the brain.

This young Peeress in her own ht is no novice in the realms of fiction, for she is the ilthor of a volume of fanciful and poetical tales, and fir written many short stories for the magazines. She c()W engaged in superintending the rehearsals of a tO" pm ct p she has written, entitled "The Finding of tti" °word," which is to be produced at a matinee at ibtecald of the month. The Countess takes a great hat 4et, in matters relating to spiritualism. Most of iiltA'aort stories are upon occult topics, and the same aii:lest attaches to her play, in which the events as er„ebut be supposed, take place in Scotland. Lady • kartie who is still on the sunny side of thirty, is a dark, handsome woman, with a bright, animated lo,atier, and is devoted to all things Scottish. She togrried Major Blunt in 1899, some six years after she alicceeded to her father's estates, which made her one of ,The largest women landowners in the limited Kingdom. It was intimated that "The Mikado" was Iseleotionable to the Japanese, and in view of the pre- of the distinguished visitor, who is returning the it-t 4 of Prince Arthur of Connaught to Japan last year, was decided to abandon its revival. The Prince is tile adopted brother of the Mikado, who, to the Japanese tenple, is not only royal but ancred. The " Mikado " bas4therefore given way, and its place has been taken aZ, Patience." This piece was first produced in 1881, 14 was written to satirise the passing craze of of theticis but although that cult has gone the way ost mfollies, the play has always been regarded tPMecially in the provinces, as one of the best of the Ilbert and Sullivan comic operas.lie • I Longevity of Pensioners.—The proverbial kligevity of pensioners was illustrated in the case of teal Robb, who died the other day in Edinburgh, at (1,8 age of ninety-four. She was the posthumous b,:11,/iliter of Captain Robb, of the Royal Navy, and was on the State pension roll at birth. One of the itt/tableincidents of her long life was her meeting, when echool-girl, with the great novelist Sir Walter Scott. If' is however in the United States that the most serearka.ble instances of the longevity of pensioners :ere to occur. Incredible as it may appear, it was only • months ago, that the last of the widows of men took part in the war of Independence in 1775 died, wiailst three women, daughters of soldiers who served tinder Washington, are still on the 'United States Derision roll. ist3lle Happiest Day.—One of the many questions 6, for solution by newspaper correspondence. is t_nnat is the happiest day in a woman's life ? " The .;S)piest people, no doubt, are those who take short allap aws of life, and among women blessed with such a •tioSition, the popular answer just now would he the iitY,abe finished spring-cleaning. The discussion is not 1,;43,3' to lead to any useful result, but it is of course _ tended to diseover,the supreme day of one's whole .7xistence. Girls in the roseate dawn of their youth, 7.0.u1d most likely think of their future wedding day, _at not a few married women would say that you have aNvnit results, before you can be sure. Still the day :Y_Fen the bride appears at the altar is also the occasion When she leaves all her old clothes behind her, and that hap contribute not a littlq to the making of the sAiest day. what makes the happiest day in a woman's life, except it is buying a new hat, or spending a successful day at the bargain sales. The question evidently does not admit of a simple or general answer. Perhaps the happiest day is like many other blessings, always to , come, and exists only in anticipation. ! Paper Headgear.—Paper millinery is once again making its appearance, and so wonderfully is it built up ' that detection is almost impossible. Further, the majority of these paper hats are "shower proof," and of course, beautifully light in weight. In colour and style, paper millinery has made great strides during the past two years, and undoubtedly a great run will be made upon it for river and holiday wear. With its neat bows, loops, rosettes, quills, etc., all in paper, it is very smart-looking, and as regards price, a girl or woman must be impecunious indeed, if she cannot afford a few paper hats to wear during the summer. Ostrich Feather Boas.—The new ostrich feather boas are shorter than we have bad them hitherto, hut they are thicker and more bushy in the middle, and taper off towards the ends. These ends reach just below the waist, and are finished with long ropes and tassels of chenille. The effect of this feather and chenille arrange- ment is more graceful than that of the very long all- feather boa, and the price is less prohibitive. The New Sleeve.—Rucked sleeves are "in " again, • and promise this summer to oust the elbow variety somewhat from favour. T„pe new sleeve is built of airy- fairy fabrics, cut on the dillhas, and fits the arm closely, and reaches well over the wrist. It is a happy thought that perchance we may be spared some of the painful exhibitions we have had before us during the past two • or three summers, and that some women with undesir- able arms will surely be tempted to cover them up in this charming and becoming manner. 1 Footstools and Cushions.—Not so very long ago, the footstool was looked upon as only fit for invalids, and very old people.—We have however changed all that, and the fashionable drawing room just now teems with footstools. In size and shape they vary considerably, but a footstool of some description finds a place under every" con3fee " chair. In the dining room, the raised ; stool running all round beneath the table, is very much approved, and greatly appreciated, especially by those among us subject to cold feet. Cushions this year are for the Most part circular, and very large, but minus the long familiar frills. Brocad eis the favourite covering, 1 giant cord finishing the edges. div.head: WRECKED JEBBA.
div.p: THE WRECKED JEBBA.
Heavy Seas Completing Destruction

The posiiion of the Elder-Dempster liner Jebba, wrecked at Bolt Tail, has become even more hopeless, as the result of a gale from the west to south-west. The Jebba, now has a heavy list to seaward, being, indeed, practically on her beam ends, and only the masts and funnel are visible at high tide. The fore- part is submerged at all states of the tide, but as yet the hull, although rolling heavily, is apparently intact. From Hope Cove to Prawle Point the coast is lined with wreckage, large quantities of palm oil and rubber having been washed ashore. Boats from Salcombe, too, brought in about half a ton of rubber found floating loose, as well as a quantity of timber. The lifeboat on the poop deck has been carried off its skids by the seas.

Though the gracefully floating veil has been killed by its own popularity, and is to be no longer seen in the 'best shops, veils are coming in, says London Opinion, for a lot of attention, and quite a new kind of veil promises to catch the public taste. This is made of the finest mesh in bright colours ornamented with big chenille spots of a darker shade and sometimes two spots contrasting with one another, as in the ease of a light blue mesh ornamented with a dark blue and a bright emerald green spot. Ostrich feather boas are shorter this, year and made in lighter colours, finished with long silk tassels to match; while the übiquitous marabout stole again appears, this time in pure white mounted on net and trimmed all round the edges with a fan-like design of Valenciennes lace and ostrich feather trimming.

div.head: SPRING COAT.
div.p: SPRING COAT.

With the advance of spripg the vogue for the small separate coat becomes more and more marked, the coats themselves becoming ever more stylish and chic. A particularly smart little coat of this type is illustrated. in our sketch, the material employed being a light and pretty covert coating. This little coat fastens in single-breasted fashion with four large, buttons, the fronts being firmly machined at the edge.

From the neck turns back a small notched collar of the material adorned with a double row of machining. On either side of the front comes a shaped breast seam, which turns a few inches from the bottom and makes the tour of the coat about three inches from the edge. The seam is ornamented throughout its entire length witfi two rows of machining. Small neat "coat" sleeves finish in plain stitched cuffs which come right down to the wrist. CIVIL SERVICE FOR GIRLS.

It is not so very long ago, writes Josephine Buller in the Mark Lane Express, since the British Government opened its doors to women workers, and to-day nearly 12,000 of them are employed-in the Civil Service as girl and women clerks and sorters, whilst 28,000 more are counted as "partially employed." Evidently the Civil Service offers an attractive career to girls, since so many of them enter it, and a proof of its popularity with them is the fact that 300 candi- dates recently _came forward for twenty appoint- ments, despite the drawback of a fairly stiff exa- rn ination. _ .

ii;;-,avant ages offered by the Civil Service to its women employees are sufficient to explain the I competition for its posts. Although the pay. is not lordly it is sure, and there are many privi- leges which compensate to some extent for the comparatively small salary. For instance, there is a lady doctor on the staff of every large Lon- don office, and the clerks and sorters get their medical attendance and medicines free. Then, the hours are not long, leaving leisure in which an industrious girl can .a.cld something to her in- come by clever fingers or brains. And then there is a pension which she can look forward to en- joying at sixty, an age which seems too impos- sibly distant to the "girl clerk" of eighteen, but against whose disabilities she one day begins to feel thankful that she is provided. In the matter of illness, too, the Government deals generously with its women workers. Should they fall ill their pay is continued for six months. If they are not then sufficiently recovered to resume work they receive half pay for the next six months, and if at the end of that time they are still unable to resume work they are allowed to retire with a small pension. A breakdown whilst in the Civil Service that incapacitates a woman for further work is always mitigated by a small pension. And should all go well with the clerk, and the cause of her leaving work be the pleas- anter one of marriage, she is given a "marriage portion" .1:1sy. the Government she has served.
-It should' be noted, however, that she must have held a post for at least six years before be- coming eligible for any of these monetary privileges.
MADEMOISELLE'S BLOUSE,

Now that Easter is behind U 6 we begin to feel that but a very short time separates us from the end of the term, and that before we realise it we shall have our youngsters home again, all, probably, badly in need of new attire. It is with a view to the special requirements of mademoiselle that the charming blouse pictured in our sketch has been designed. Of dainty

printed cambric, the little shirt will wash and launder admirably, and is altoggther a most practical and useful garment fdi school wear. Down the middle of the front runs a plain box pleat, stitched at both • edges, and adorned with buttons. On either side of the centre pleat on the shoulders come six inverted tucks, which are stitched down to just below the armhole and then released, the resultant fulness being drawn down to the waist. The sleeves, of the bishop shape, are taken into rather deep stitched cuffs at the wrist. ___

div.head: LONELY WOMEN.
div.p: LONELY WOMEN.

Who. asks Miss E. G. Turnbull in Woman, wants a lonely woman? So also cries the un- attached one. It is your own fault if you are lonely. Loving and sympathetic women are al- ways wanted; the world is hungry for, them. Ent you must prove your mettle first. Nobody is going to offer you love until they see that you have something to give for it. You might as well open a shop without any stock and then grumble because nobody comes to buy.

div.p: THE DISTRESS COMMITTEE.

On the proposition of Alderman TINNION, seconded by Councillor WlLKinsas, the following were elected co-optative members on the Distress Committee : Mrs. Joseph Harrison, the Rev. W. Bracecamp, the Rev. John Yonge, Mr. John Haley and Mr. T. P. Bradshaw.
MEDICAL OFFICER OF HEALTH. A QUESTION OF SALARY.

At a special meeting of the Health Committee held on March 19th, the appointment of a medical officer of health was considered. It was decided that the person appointed should, in addition to covering the duties imposed by Parliament or prescribed by the Local Government Board, act as superintendent of the Coun- cil's isolation hospitals, as medical officer to the Educa- tion Committee, with certain specified duties; be responsible for the carrying out of the provisions of the Midwives Act; superintend the work of the Inspector of Nuisance; and direct and be responsible for the work of the Public Health Department; and generally discharge such other duties in relation to the above offices as the Council may from time to time require. It was resolve:l to advertise inviting applica- tions for the appointment of medical officer of health,at a salary of £450 per annum, from duly qualified medianl men, not exceeding 45 years of age. Councillor STOTT moved :—" That the,minute relat- ing to the appointment of a new medical officer of health be amended by the deletion of the sum of £450, the proposed salary, and the substitution therefor of the sum of £4OO. He contended that £4OO was ample for a commencing salary. It might be argued that they could not get a sufficiently qualified man for that sum, but he was confident that there were many men who would be pleased to secure the appoint- ment. The duties were very numerous, and he did not think one individual would be able to do the whole of the work of the Council and of the Education Com- mittee, and believed that before long they would have as a Council to appoint a permanent assistant to the Medical Officer. He hoped that appointment would be made, and that the a.sistant would be mainly respansible for the inspection of the children of the elementary schools. Before long they would have legislation which would empower the education authority to appoint a medical officer to undertake the duty he had named.

Councillor WILKINsON seconded, and said that at the meeting of the Health Committee, when the matter was discussed, he said he thought £4OO was a fair amount considering the fact that they had an assistant medical officer and that the duties' of public analyst were now discharged by Mr. Ruddock. Councillor ASHCROFT : The appointment of Dr. GatElkin is only temporary? Councillor EVANS : That is so.

Councillor LORD supported, and said he considered £4OO would be ample for a commencing Wary. It had been stated that the appointment of the deputy medical officer was only temporary,but these temporary appoint- ments became permanent. (Hear,hear). No one would move her dismissal.

Councillor PEMBERTON supported, and said it was better to start the salary lower down than to try after- wards to make a reduction in a larger salary. There were hundreds of medical men practising in England who wouli be glad of £4OO. _
Councillor riAWTHORN : Does the sum of £450 include all salaries in connection with the Bduc,ation Committee?

ThedkLutoß : It does up to now. Councillor EVANS said that while the Health Corn. mittc9 had some latitude, whoever held the position must have the diploma of public health. The Com- mittee wanted one of the best ?nen they could possibly get to begin with. (Hear, hear.) The question of increase of the salary would ever rest with the com- mittee and the Council. The Council would always have it in their power to say whether the ralary should be increased or not. The appointment of the lady doctor was by no means a permanency. Councillor Dr. JOSEPH, said that as one of the mem- bei-s of the committee who proposed £5OO, be would like to say a few words. Councillor Pemberton and others had spoken as if all they had to do was to get an ordinary qualified men, but. it should be remembered that a special scientific training was needed. The Local Government Board required that in County Boroughs with over 50,000 or 60,000 inhabitants a specially good man should be selected.

Alderman TINNION said the matter was very carefully considered in committee. £5OO was proposed, then £4OO and ultimately £450 was unanimously decided upon. They were going to have an official whose responsibility would be very great. (Hear, hear.) The appointment was far more important tban a question of £s. d.; it was the health of the little ones, of the families of the town. They wanted an experienced man and he would be cheap at £450. Alderman BOLTON pointed out that the committee had, as usual, been at sixes and sevens, and had ulti- mately decided to "split the difference." It should be remembered that there would be less work for the new man to do than Dr. Gornall was responsible for. Dr. Gornall's salary when he died was at the maximum, and he could get no more, and £4OO would be amply suffi- cient for a new man. (Hear, hear.) If the work of a man who received £4OO was satisfactory he would be worth more in twelve months' time, and he (Alderman Bolton) had never seen the Corporation act in a niggarly manner in raising a man's salary when he was worth having it raised. (Hear, hear.) If it was not raised h 3 would go to another place. There were rising young men who would be 'glad to di3 the work for £4OO. ile should, therefore, support Councillor Stott's motion. There were certain men who wanted an official to wear a uniform and paid him £5O a year more to do so and tu meet Government officials.
Councillor AsHcßorr : Will the services of the lady doctor be retained when the Medical Officer is appointed? nocillor WILKINSON : Certainly.

div.head: INCREASES OF SALARY.
div.p: INCREASES OF SALARY.

At a meeting of the Health Committee it was decided that the following increases of salary be granted Percival, clerk, from 255. to 308. ; A. Isherwood, from 16s. 6d. to £1 ; and J. Hands, porter, 16s. to 18s. The minutes were approved, on the motion of Coun- cillor EVANS, seconded by Councillor BURTON. The Paving and Sewerage Committee also decided to increase the wages of Mr. Sydney Bolton from 30s. to 355. per week, and the wages of Mr. H. S. 3aulter from 295. to 355. per week. THE LAWSON CONTRACT WRIT.

The Town Clerk reported to a recent meeting of the Water Committee that be had been served with a writ for £36,425 is. at the suit of Mr. George Lawson, being the balance claimed of his account for work done and materials supplied. It was resolved that the Town Clerk be instructed to defend the action.
The committee's minutes were adopted. on the propo- sition of Alderman TINNION, seconded by Councillor DUNCAN.

PROPOSED EXTENSIONS AT HOWLEY DEPOT The Sanitary Works Committee visited Longford, Howley, and Hardy-street Depots and resolved that the Borough Surveyor be requesteo to prepare plans and estimate of the cost of the proposed alterations and extensions at Howley Depot. Alderman EVANS in moving the adoption of the minutes said last year was a record as far as the sales of manure were concerned. Councillor CH&NTLEIt said the inhabitants of the Howley district were strongly opposed to an extension of the depot. They thought these favours should be equally divided. (Laughter.) Alderman EVANS said the matter was entirely in the initiative stage. All they had done was to ask for an estimate of the cost.
The minutes were approved. STRONG CRITICISM OF STREET REPAIRS.

In moving the adoption of the minutes of the Paving and Sewerage Committee, Alderman rinnion said Mr. Owen had withdrawn a tender for paving certain streets and the committe had requested Mr. Thomas Stringer to undertake the work. Mr. Owen's tender was for £4651 Ts. and Mr. Stringer's, which was the next lowest, amounted to £4,858. Councillor WILDING asked whether the accounts passed for payment included sams in respect of the repaving of Hale-street, off Longford-street. Alderman TIN. NEON: lam not a walking encyclopmlia. I would be only too pleased to give the information if I could, but it would be more courteous of Councillor Wilding to give notice of the question. Councillor WILDING regretted that he had not had the opportunity of giving notice,as the matter was only mentioned to him that morning. He would like to know how long it was since the street was made in th, first instance. He was given to understand it was within recent years, and if that were so be would be glad to know whose fault it was that they had to re-pave it so soon. The re-paving of streets was a terrible strain on the rates of Warrington. The MAYOR : You are putting a terrible strain on this Council. (Laughter.) It would be far better for you to submit the question in writing before the next meeting. COUTIOIIIOL PEMBERTON held that if a Councillor thought a payment bad been improperly made, be had a right to move that it be not passed. This was the third time the street bad been paved within five years. It was a very serious question. The Corporation had paid for miles of streets which in a few years were a dis- grace. The worst feature was that the private owners paid their share in order that the street might he repaired with proper material and workmanship, and serious notice ought to be taken of the question. The TOWN CLERK said the standin,, orders required that notice of questions should b: given. He was informed that the accounts passed for payment/did not include the cost of repairing Hale-street. The work had been done since March 25th. Alderman Trgsrox said there were not miles of streets in Warrington which had been paved and which were unfit for anyone to walk through in a few years. T:ie pay,ing of Warrington streets was better than that in any other manufacturing town in Lancashire. CollDoilior WILDING: It is questionable. The minutes were appreved. THE SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Rivers Committee presented a long report on the Manchester Ship Canal (Various Powers) Bill. ln addition to the petition of the Corporation the follow- ing firms also petitioned against the Bill :—Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Ltd., ,Monks Hall and Company,Ltd. James Fairclough and Sons, Ltd„ Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company. Ltd., Rvlands Bros. Ltd.. Whitecross Company, Ltd. The Bill was passed by the committee of thG House of Lords but clauses safe- guarding Warrington with regard to the height of spoil banks, &c.P were inserted. The Bill as amended would go before the committee of the House of Commons during April. It was considered advisable that the Corporation should be represented when the Bill was in committee, and therefore a petition against the Rill should be presented. It was resolved that a petition be presented to the House of Commons against the Manchester Ship Canal Bill, 1907. The minutes were confirmed, on the motion of Alderman BoLTON, seconded by Alderman BENNETT. "LIFE DESTROYING ENGINE."

When the minutes of the Fire Engine Committee came up for approval Councillor Wilding asked if there was any information with reference to the new life- destroying chemical engine. (Laughter). Had the Corporation to pay for it? The MAYOR.: It is not advisable to discuss the ques- tion now. You will hava another opportunity— Councillor EVANS : Of examining the machine. (Laughter.) THE STANDARD RATE QUESTION.

COUNCILLOR STOTT AND A LOCAL CONTRACT. At a meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Com- mittee the following letter from the St. Helens Cable Co., Ltd., was read : Warrington. 7th March. 1907. Dear Sir,—ln reply to your letter of the 6th. I have pleasure in stating that we do pay the standard rate of wages and observe the recognised hours of labour which are considered fair in our trade in this district.—Yours faithfully, For the St. Helens Clble Co. Ltd.,.. F. ICENYON:Secretary.

Resolved, that the order for cables according to 'the tender accepted be placed with the St. Helens Cable Co„ Ltd. Councillor STOTT said it would appear from a pN.usal of the letter that the statements be made at the last meeting were incorrect, hut he was prepared to repast what he then stated and to give other instances of the conditions of labour obtaining under the firm. He said distinctly that those conditions did not comply with the Standing Orders and that the letter was worth just about as much as the Standing Orders were worth if the com- mittees were not going to carry them out in the spirit in which they were passed by the Council. The objec- tions which he had were that the firm attempted to use the labour bureau to obtain joiners and pay them 255. A week-15s. or 16s. a week less than the trade union and standard rate for 'Warrington. The engineers employed there some time ago had to withdraw all their members from that firm because they gave notice of a reduction of wages which brought the rate below the standard. A short time ago three members of the Operative Plumbers' Union, qualified men, in answer to an advertisement made application to the firm and were told that the wages would be 7d. adhour and that the firm would not under any consideration pay more. The minimum rate they ought to pay, if they were going to pay the standard rate, was 81d. He did not consider the committee had acted fairly in letting the firm go on with the contract after receiving a letter which simply stated that they observed the customary hours of labour and paid the standard rate. It was possible for the Corporation to give work to some of the worst sweating firms in the country if those firms were prepared to write a letter stating that the conditions at their works were fair. The cemmittee ought to make some reasonable inquiry. He had not the slightest animosity against that or any other firm in-Warrington but he wanted the Standing Orders adhering to. He could assure the Council that if any further contract were given to the firm and they did not adhere to the Standing Orders, the whole of the Labour movement in Warrington would strongly object to the action of the Council. He did not offer this as a threat, but he knew the feel- ing of the workingmen.iie regretted very much to have to complain about a local firm because he was anxious

to get all the work he could for Warrington working- men but it w•)rild not, be fair, even from the employers' standpoint, to let the matter pass on that ground. It had been argued that the employees he had enumerated were notactnally emnloyed in the tr.ide or cable making or the manufacture of electrical eluipment, hot he con- sidered that argument was ridiculoas. F-11 cl Li rnq 1 that any employee of a firm was engseed in the manufactnre of the particular commodity which that firm sold. If they were going to whittle it down to the manufacture O f insulated cables, it might be possible that only a few girls or youths were engaged in fee3inz the machines.
ELECTRICITY EXTENSION. £9,000 TO BE SPENT.

Mr. F. V. L. MATHIAS. borough electrical and tram- ways engineer, stibmitted a report to a recent meeting of the Electricity and Tramways Committee on the need for boiler plant axtension. The estimated cost is £8,704, and for electrical plant £350. The MAYOR moved the adoption of the minutes. and said it was imnerative they should extend the electric light works. For some time the boilers had been doing double work. The committee were constantly havin^ applications for current, but they could nn S supply any more customers 'until the extensions were carried out. C(.llmcillor WrucissoN secon'ed.

_ Alderman BOLTON remarked that seeing they were spending £9,000 in extensions, they might see if they could not reduce the price of electricity for lighting purposes. They made 400 per cent. oat of the ordinary consumers, and gave it to those who used electricity for . power purposes. Conncillor LORD said the ordinary consumers had to pay Pnorinous charges. It. was a gioss scandal to let manufacturers have electricity at cost price or below cost price at the expense of other customers. Councillor PEMBERTON said those who used elec- tricity for lighting purposes paid 43. per unit SS ' I against d. paid by those requiring it for power pur- poses. It WAS monstrous, as all ratepayers had a right to he equally considered. Power ought to have a . preference, but not to the present extent. They did not. make any profit out of power customers, which wasdi an injustice to other ratepayers. He contended it would pay to put electric light into workmen's homes at :7d., and why should they not have the benefit of it? Councillor WILKINSON pointed out that their work- men and engines would be idle in the day time unless they supplied the manufacturers who paid cost price. Warrington sold electricity for lighting purposes as cheaply as any borough in England. Councillor Pember- ton had retired from the Electricity Commitcee, and placed himself in a position to attack, RS he always did. : Councillor LORD interjected a remark, whereupon , Councillor Wilkinson said :—" You will never get me down, Lord." ' Impudence and cheek, he continued, he : could always stand, because be could answer back in the ' same way.

The MAYOR : Order. Go outside, and you can put the gloves on. (Laughter). Continuing, the Mayor said they supplied no one at id. They were selling to consumers for lighting purposes at rates cheaper than Nlanchester and most of the towns in England. As regarded the price for power, they were as cheap, or cheaper than Bolton, Manchester and Liverpool. (Hear, hear). It was continuation of work they must have to make a profit. Warrington, he contended, gave more advantages to the public than any other town in Lanca- shire.

Councillor PEMBERTON : What does it cost us per unit, for capital charges and working expenses? The MAYOR: You might go in opposition to us, and build a new works. (Laughter). The minutes were adopted.

THE APPOINTMENT OF CHIEF CONSTABLE. The General Purposes Committee resolved that the Watch Committee be authoris6d to advertise fzur a Chief Constable at £350 per annum, on the understanding that the name of the person selected by that Committee be submitted to this Committee. _
Councillor STorr naked whether the Council would have power to sanction at disapprove of the appoint- ment.
The MAYOR said the appointment wouH be brought before the Council for confirmation._

COilllOniqr EVANS, who moved the above resolution, said it was his intention that the name should be sub- mitted to the General Purposes Committee for approval. The minutes were confirmed. PROPOSED PROFESSIONAL AUDITOR.

The Finance and Estate Committee resolved that a professional auditor be appointed under Section 164 of ,the Warrington Corporation Act, 1899, to audit the accounts of the Corporation, and that his duties and salary be deferrel for further consideration.

Alderman INNNErr, in moving the adoption of the minutes, said the question of a professional auditor had been under the consideration of the Council ever since he was a member. Latterly, at the suggestion of Councillor Ball, they had obtained a good deal of information as to what other towns did, and they had decided to have a professional auditor. He was entirely in favour of the principle. In undertakings of the immense magnitude of the Corporation it was extremely desirable that they should have the best auditor they could get. The existing law was so complicated that he was inclined to defer the matter a little longer to see if anything came of the recommendations of the Special Committee on Municipal Trading. If they appointed a professional auditor at the present stage it meant that they would have to continue to appoint elective auditors and. presnmably,to pay them and there would also be a Mayor's auditor. That would be ridiculous. The whole vestion would come before them again. He believed that if the ratepayers always appointed properly qualified professional men no serious harm would be done under the existing conditions. Aldermen FonsYrkw seconded. Councillor PEMBERTON said the minute meant that they were going to appoint a professional auditor, and he moved, as an amendment, that the minute be not passed. The MAYOR observed that the Town Clef* informed him they could not appoint an auditor until they had fixed the salary and defined the duties.

Alderman BE'CNETT said they ought to have absolute security that thA accounts were thoroughly audited every year. There was no guarantee in the present system, and the electors might choose to elect men who had no professional qualifications whatever. Councillor PENfIITTRTON said the Manchester Corpora- tion emploped some of finest accountants in England, and the peculiar thing was that when any scandal arose their plid auditors never discovered one single thing. How much good had the auditors been to limited com- panies which had gone to the wall. The accounts had been acclited by men who were above suspicion but who had been misled. The Corporation officials, so far as the Borough Treasurer's department was concerned, could andit the:r arcn-ints. He agreed with Alderman Bennett that they ought to wait and see what the committee on municipal trading were going to do. Alderman BENNI:TT said the Corporation had three or four businesses in one and the accounts ought to be scrutinised by an expert."He would not waste breath on Councillor Pemberton' innuendoes. The profession to which he belonged was one. of the most honourabTe, and would compare with any other profession in the country. Councillor PEMBERTON said he did not make any charges against incorporated accountants. Their honour was above question. Alderman BENNETT withdrew the minute. and with this exception the committee's minutes were passed.

div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

THE PARISH INSTITUTE.—A general body of the members and friends attached to; the above met at the Institute; called by special circular to discuss the advisability of either closing it or carrying it on. It appears that the Institute during the past season has been badly supported, the members apparently not taking sufficient interest in it. Ultimately a com- mittee was formed to find a solution of the difficulty.

div.head: SHOT TN AN HOTEL.
div.p: SHOT TN AN HOTEL.

The man who as found shot in a Southsea hotel on Sunday morning has been identified as Leo Farmer botany expert at Kew Gardens, who was expecting to go on an expedition under Sir Alfred Jones to Africa to investigate the possibilities of cotton growing thele. TOO INQUISITIVE.

Two men were seen by the Chief Chief Constable of Tunbridge wells fighting desperately. He parted them, and they then asked him to act as referee in order to order to decide which had had the better of the tussle. When taken to the station they offered to bail each other out.

div.head: AGED 103 YEARS!
div.p: AGED 103 YEARS!

Mrs. Hannah Bursnall, of Skillington near. Gratham, on Thursday attained her 103rd birthday. She was born at Wymondham, was married when 23, and had 14 children. She has about 40 grandchildren and several great grand-children.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
APRIL 13th. 1907
The Tariff Reformers are THE making the most it is PREFERENCE possible to make for their CAMPAIGN. cause out of the visit of the

visit of the Colonial Premiers Such of those distinguished gentlemen as have yet arrived in England have already had several opportunities of denying stories that have been put about in the interests of Tariff Reform. It has been said, for example, with every• adornment of " scare-headings " and displayed typo, that if the Government does not meet their wishes with regard to Preference, they will hold a private conference of their own by way ot demonstration against his Majesty's Ministers. The tale is a pure invention, with malice at the bottom of it. It is an item in the programme drawn up by the Tariff Reformers for the express purpose, as it would seem, of embroil- ing us with out Colonies. To such a low deno mination has patriotism sunk, with those who- mouth it the most and profess to be its apostles and defenders!

Since Tariff Reform came in there has been an altogether remarkable decline in intellectual honesty. It seems to be assumed that a mis- representation, an equivocation, or even a positive felsehood, requires no justification if it serves the purpose of deceiving those whom it is intended to deceive. That is justification enough in itself. We take the latest example of the sort of means employed to influence public opinion in favour of Tariff Reform. On Wednesday night a (London evening paper of the Chamberlainite school invited the attention of the Colonial Premiers to the fact that thousands of English " black- legs " are working in the port of Hamburg, where there is a strike of labourers. That is a fact which of course, we must all lament, just as we must welcome the return of so many of these men when they found out what they had been taken over to Germany for. But there is no lamentation on the part of our Tariff Refurrn contemporary. There is rejoicing, on the contrary, for the reason that the taking over of these English mer- cenaries to Hamburg is assumed to prove that whilst there is a vast amount of unem- ployment in our own counft7, there is none at all in Germany, because Germany is a Protec tionist country, and we are ourselves setting the world an example in freedom of trade. "These men," it is remarked of those who are blackiegging at Hamburg, "are drawn from that melancholy residium of workers waifs who would find that bread was as cheap at home if they had something to buy it with." Not the slightest proof of this statement is oflered, of course, and for good enough reasons.

The men who have been taken over to Hamburg are experienced dock labourers. The bulk of them it is probable, have been taken from actual work. They have been tempted by those higher wages which are always offered by employers who are fighting a strike. During the nine hours' day- strike in the North of Englani engineering trade, more than thirty years ago,Germans were brought over in the same way, to be employed in our engineering shops. They went back again when they found out the facts of the situation) just as the dock labourers are coming back from Hamburg now. What thoroughly conscious dis- ingenuousness there must be in founding a corn parison between the industrial condition of Germany and of England on such an incident as this! And in any case, what ground can there at present be for a comparison unfavourable to ourvelves ? If trade returns moan anything at all, those which we are now receiving indicate an almsst unprecedented national prosperity.

A second successive reduc- RATES AND tion in the borough rates PROOREss. of 4d. in the should put all Warrington ratepayers in a good humour. We hinted last week that a substantial reduction would be announced at Tuesday's Council meeting, and for once in a way a prophecy came true. "Never prophesy unless you know " is a good maxim and one that we took care to abide by. As a matter of fact we could have announced the amount of the reduction last week, for even good tidings fly apace sometimes, but consideration for Alderman Bennett's feelings prompted us to withold the figures. We hope the Deputy-Chancellor of the Exchequer will be duly grateful. His budget speech on Tuesday was a model of conciseness, intelligibility, and inter- est. He traversed the dry and stony desert of figures with a light step, cheered on by the goal in front. Of course the Alderman walked in a roseate glow, which was reflected in all he said. We agree with him that it is a municipal achievement to have brought about a steady and continuous decrease in the rates from 7s. 10d. in 1904-6 to 7s. to-day, concurrently with an increase in the expenditure on education, but in praising the officials and the ratepayers for this satisfactory state of things, Alderman Bennett did not go quite Sir Alexander Swettenham far enough. There is a body of gentlemen one : THAT JAMAICA is a puszle to most people. time known as Non-Traders, who applied the brake I INCIDNNT. His resignation of the post at the right time and steadied the municipal coach of Governor of Jamaica) no when it threatened to go headlong down the hill one doubted, was due to the incident which had taken place with the American Admiral. The

to insolvency. Alderman Bennett was occasionally at variance with the reformers in the days of their greatest activity, but we believe that he himself will admit that no inconsiderable part of the ceedit for the happy condition of things t,-day is due to their efforts in checking expenditure. At any rate, be has come to a similar way of thinking for it is to ba noted that speaking of the future, Alderman Bennett said "he hoped they would proceed in that policy and go slowly and cautiously." This is significant counsel from the Deputy-Chancellor, and the affirmative spirit in which it was received indicates that the danger of the municipality getting out of hand is past. A vista of prosperity and progress seems to be gradually opening out, and Warrington should, with its natural advantages and a continuance of sound policy, rise rapidly to a position of unsurpassed commercial eminence in the County Palatine.

"The reduction in the rates PROFITS AND does not " to quote STOCK-IN-TRADE. Alderman Bennett again "represent the whole of our internal stock-in-trade of satisfaction." It is worthy of remembrance that the reduction is possible in the face of an increased call for educa- tional purposes of 2d in the 2, is concurrent with a reduction of 2d. per 1,000 cubic feet in the price of ga3 ; and that without the education call, the rates would only be ss. Bd. in the L, a sum much below the average for the last 50 years. Then, too, as municipal traders we people of Warrington have a right to indulge in some self-praise. Five of our main departments—capitalised at something like a million pourfds—earned last year a gross profit of £55,916 which is equal to a dividend of over 5 per cent. The sum received from the Gas and Markets Committees alone in relief of the rates was £16,382, which is the largest amount received from similar sources in any town in England with the exception of Naturally, therefore, Alderman Bennett invited the members of the Council "to face the fat ore with becoming cheerfulness." Under the Icircumstances it should not be difficult. The balance sheet of the borough seems to be in a healthy condition, and there is a Council at the head of affairs which has got over sectional differences and is working unitdly towards a common end—the greatest good of the greatest number.
, The withdrawal on Tuesday THE BOROUGH of the Finance Committee's AUDIT. recommendation to appoint

a professional audito-rs was undoubtedly the wisest course seeing that the whole question may have to be re-opened when the Parliamentary Special Committee on muni- cipal trading has concluded its deliberations. We over-looked this important consideration when we expressed, in our issue last week, the hope that the recommendation would be confirmed. It is of course essential that the borough accounts should be professionally audited and as a rule they are, but there is no guarantee that under the existing law the ratepayers might not elect auditors who lacked the necessary qualifica- tions to do the work thoroughly. Tha appoint- ment of a professional man by the Corporation would obviate this difficulty, but it might lead to others. We believe that this is not the kind of audit which the Non-Traders and other municipal reformers are agitating for. A borough auditor of the kind mentioned would ensure professional accuracy, but his hands would be, to some extent, tied by whose who appointed him and paid his salary. At least one other independent auditor would be essential. The best solution to the whole difficulty would be the audit of municipal accounts by Government officials, who would have not only the liberty to point out irregularities but the power to surcharge the responsible committees or individuals also. The accounts of rural authori- ties are audited in this way and if such a safeguard is essential in the smaller it must of necessity be doubly essential in the greater local authorities. The recommendations of the Parliamentary Com- mittee will be awaited with interest, and in the meantime Warrington's best policy is a waiting policy.

For some years Warrington THE HORSE has, in common with many PARADE. other industrial centres, organized a May celebration in the form of a procession of horses. It would be difficult to over-estimate the good which such an annual event must do in encouraging owners and drivers of horses to keep them in the best possible condition, and we are glad that the Com- mittee have decided to hold another parade on May 25th. Successful as previous shows have been, we believe they might be made a great deal more popular, as far as the general public are concerned. On several occasions attention has been called in this journal to the pronounced lack of original or specially attractive features in the pro- cession. It is indeed pleasing to see a long suc- cession of well-fed, smartly groomed horses, but to the average " man in the street the display is apt to become monotonous. We are sure that by offering prizes for the most taste- fully and ingeniously decorated turnouts the committee would do a great deal to enhance the interest of the parade as a spectacle. The public would be pleased and as a result the charities on behalf of which the committee so considerately makes a collection would benefit more substantially. We hope that competitors will assist in providing a pageant more in keeping with "the merrie month" and that the horse parade of 1907 may be accounted the most successful on record.

The agitation of Mrs. Pank- THE hurst and her daughter. 3 SUFFRAGETTES. and their friends has not been without results. It may be useful to specify some of these, First of all, it has closed to women a part of the Palace of Wedtminster to which they might always find entrance, for they were well-behaved. The central hall, the great circular space between the lobbies leading to the doors of the House of Commons, has been easily accessible to ladies. Women with a grievance have "lobbied " there unmolested for day after day and for month after month, and sometimes for years on end. There was an amusing old lady who believed that she was the real owner of Hyde Park, and who demanded four millions from the Chancellor of the Exchequer as compensation from the public by which it had been appropriated. Her intention, she declared, was to divide the four million pounds between the policemen on duty at the House as a recognition of the kindness which they had invariably shown in her. It was, besides, a favourite place with the mere sightseer. Mem- bers of both Houses of Parliament were constantly passing through. Distinguished men of all sorts came down to the House and passed through the central hall on their way to the members' lobby. There was no such place for setting eyes for a brief moment on the great personalities of the day. But all this has been changed, so far as women are concerned, through the action of the suffragettes. The " sex " is now admitted to the central hall only under difficult conditions. Even the wives of Minister of the Crown are not per- mitted to pass through the doors leading out of St. Stephen's Hall unless they are accompanied by a member of one of the two Houses. Whether such a result as this was worth producing, the suffragettes may well set themselves to consider. Other results of the agitation are the dis- covery that only a small number of women are desirous of enfranchisement; that the women who do desire have so little sense of humour that they engage girls of 15 or 16 years of age to march on the House of Commons and demand the vote; and that they are grievously lacking in logic and in the power of accurate statement. There is, however, something to be said on the other side. Undoubt- edly the interest of the public in the woman's franchise question lips been awakened into keen ness, but whether women will be enfranchised any sooner in consequence is open to grave doubt.

div.p: letter which he had written to Admiral Davis was to say the least, indiscreet. It erred in several ways, but chiefly—to take the most lenient view of it—in the direction of treating 'with levity a very serious subject. Admiral -Davis did not act, perhaps, as inter- national courtesy required in landing his troops without a request. Nor can one altigether acquit him of blame in ralation to the publication to the Press of a letter which was obviously Private, and certainly ought not to have been banded to the newspapers without an intimation to the author of the letter that such a course was to be taken. However that may he, Sir Alexander himself acted in a somewhat extraordinary fashion, and his friends in this conntry are not assisted in presenting his case by his method of tendering his resignation. They have con- tended all along that the Colonial Office was concealing the true cause of the retirement by representing Sir Alexander as being relieved on the ground of age. Yet here is his own telegram sent after the demand had been made that he should apologise to the American: "Respectfully apply tr permission for retirement on account of age." L'hY Sir Alexander should have deliberately chosen ;0 give a reason which was not the true reason for nia action is a mystery that will baffle most people, unless he yielded to what appears to be a sort of Passion with him, and the telegram, like his letter, „was, as Artemus Ward would say," wrote sarcastic." Whatever the explanation, the result is to weaken hat CRSO he had against the Government, and the best that can now happen is that his friends shall .allow the matter to rest exactly where his own telegram has placed it. As Mr, Churchill said, delicate questions are involved in the correspond- ence which has taken place, and the recapitulation Of the whole business might be fraught with diffi- culties which could not be met without giving unnecessary offence across the Atlantic. Sir a-lexander wrote the letter to Admiral Davies rashly, and probably regretted it sincerely. It will n,c't mend matters to indulge in recrimination on tills side.

The other day he was standing in the entrance hall of his club when a new member Went up to him and asked, "I beg your pardon, sir, but do you happen to have seen a gentleman, one of the members of this club, with a glass eye called Matthew ? From " London Opinion." * A day out in the country at this time of the year is not only very pleasant but also refreshing as well, for sweet scents from budding nature pervade the air. But at Padgate station this week, the scents have been anything but pleasant and refreshing owing to the close proximity of the goods siding which is immedi- ately behind the platform where passengers depart for Warrington. We would suggest that the luggage vans containing the manure for farmers should be relegated to another siding—at least 400 yards away, so as to prevent a recurrence of the nuisance. Perhaps , the Padgade Parish Council who do not appear to be overburdened with work will take the matter up -or will the district Council ? Many complaints have been heard—to say nothing of strong and unprintable language. -

* In 1807, when England had a quarrel with the Northern Powers, the Chancelloi of the Exchequer,Al r Vansittart, made it practically impossible to obtain Baltic timber at all. He almost entirely repealed the duties on timber coming from our American possessions, and placed an enormous duty on North European timbers. We were to be made independent of the foreigner, and to become a self sufficing empire in the matter of timber. The immediate result of the policy was that we were flooded for years with inferior timber from Canada ; the good, cheap timber from the North of Europe was shut out, and we were compelled to use for build- ing purposes wood particularly subject to dry-rot. But there was still a demand for Baltic timber, and there followed one of those absurdities which always track the course of Protection. It actually paid to ship wood from Northern Europe to Canada in order that it might come in here as colonial timber. In consequence of this artificial stimulus, large vested interests grew up in Canada in connection with the trade. When the preference was withdrawn these interests not unnaturally raised piercing cries, declared themselves certain to be ruined, threatened secession, and agitated in favour of annexation with the United States.—.T. St. Lee Straclacy.
