div.head: Latchford Wesley Guild.
div.p: Latchford Wesley Guild.

At the meeting beld in the Wesleyan Church on Thursday evening, Miss Ethel Ford being in the chair, a paper was read by Mr. Hugh Ronnals on "Heroes." Several well known and notable examples were cited by the essayist in which military and naval men and civilians have figured as " heroes." A short discussion followed the reading of the.paper.

PREMIER IN NAME, Premier in quality. Premier Cycles from seven guineas.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Municipal Officer's Guild. The first function in connection with the socia section of the above Society, in the shape of a whist drive was held on Thursday evening, at Atkinson's Cafe, about 50 members and friends being present. The social committle have every reason to feel satis- fied with this their first meeting. The M.C. for the evening was Mr. 11. Warburton, and Mrs. J. 'Fairhurst distributed the prizes to the winners at the close of the evening. The presence of ladies was a pleasing feature, and all thoroughly enjoyed then;tselves. "Trial by Jury." Last evening the members of Crosfield's choir and orchestra gave a successful performance of the Gilbert-Sullivan operetta "Trial by Jury" in the works dining hall. There was a large attendance and the production was highly appreciated. There were full stage effects and pretty costumes. The chief characters were :—plaintiff, Miss C. Hastings ; defendant, Mr. W. Tynan; judge, Mr. E. Walker; counsel, Mr. D. B. Ardern and Mr. H. Cook; usher, Mr. E. Willams ; attorney, Mr. G. Gleaye. Mr. F. J. Lord conducted, whilst Mr. T. Knowles acted as stage manager.

Beautiful Warrington Society. The first distribution of plants held last Saturday attracted only two or three applicants, partly perhaps owing to want of publicity, and partly because of the weather, and very little therefore was dispensed out of the stock, which had been recently increased by donations from Mr. T. Crampton, Bridge-street, and Mrs. Broadbent, and by a valuable consignment from Mrs. J. Crosfield, of Colwyn Bay, including geraniums and other bedding plants, and a number of aspidistras in pots. One consequence of the failure will be that there will be a large stock for the next distribution which will take place on Saturday, the 27th inst., from three to four. It cannot be too widely known that every member is qualified to participate.

div.head: UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Padgate District Norse Association.
div.p: UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Padgate District Norse Association.

On Thursday night in the National Schools, Padgate, a successful concert and dramatic perform- ance was held on behalf of the above association. There was a large at d appreciative audience, and the funds of the association will receive a much needed help. The artistes in the dramatic performance all performed their various parts creditably. Mr. Barnes andiMiss E. Royston especially shining. TheAcertainly showed histrionic ability above the average. In the miscellaneous programme Mr. Owen as the humonrist fairly brought down the house, whilst Dr. Bennett, Miss Owen; and "Mrs. Atkin were encored. Mr. Blackwell was an efficient pianist.

div.head: Former Warrington Gentleman's Fatal Fall.
div.p: Former Warrington Gentleman's Fatal Fall.

Many Warrington people will regret to hear of the death of Mr. John James Fairhurst, a native of this town, who died at Southport this week under sad circumstances. The deceased gentltnaan, who was forty-five years of age, was a son of the late Mr. Hugh Fairhurst, chemist, Warrington, and up to leaving Warrington about fifteen'years ago he resided at Heath- field, Latchford. He went to live in retirement at SO, Leyland-road, Southport, where the accident which resulted in his death took place. On Tuesday night Mr. Fairhurst was going upstairs when he fell and fractured his skull, dying shortly atterwards. At the inquest on Thursday evening a verdict of " Accidental death" was returned. The funeral will take place at the Warrington Cemetery at 12.30 to-day (Saturday). PCTLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER Tun CLOCK TO BEI BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt.

Watered Milk. William Littlefair, Orford-lane, Warrimzton, was summoned at the Borough Court, yesterday, for having sold milk which was adulterated with 10 per cent of water.—lnspector Flood deposed to purchasing a quart of new milk from the defendant in Sharp-, street on the morning of March 14. He divided it in the usual way, and on a sample being analysed by Mr. Ruddock it was found to have been adulterated with 10 per cent of water.— Mr. Steel, for the defence, said Littlefair had been in the milk business for four years, during which time Inspector Flood had frequently taken samples, and had found them to be all right. On the date in question defendant ran short of milk, and he pur- chased a quantity from other dealers, which he mixed iwith his own. He had always conducted his business in an honest way, and had never any intention of adulteration.—A fine of 20s. and costs was inflicted.

Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., at a Labour meeting at Black- brook, St. Helens, on Saturday night welcomed the reduction of the navy in prospect of the Hague Con- ference, and said that so far as the navy was concerned he was convinced that they had all the security they , required. When he came to the Territorial Army Bill he was not so sanguine. He did not like many of its clauses. The volunteer force had been a civilian army and they had been no discredit to the fighting forces of • the country, as they showed during the Boer war. Be objected to the civilian character of the volunteer force being taken away. Under the Territorial Army Bill

He remem- bered the War Office during the Boer war, and he was not over-sanguine in committing to their exclusive care the management of the home defences. He remembered the bungling of the officers during the fighting and the incompetency of the men in charge of the food and the requirements of the soldiers, and if the War Office were going to treat the home force with the same lack of efficiency as they did the fighting the force in South Africa it would be Heaven help the British army. (Cheers.) Under the new scheme the schools of the aristocracy, Eton and Harrow, were to have cadet corps, or volunteer corps, and the sons of rich men who went to those schools were to be drilled with the avowed intention that when they left the school they would have a commission given to them in the British army. He objected to this, because he said that in every public service the only ladder of promo- tion should be that of ability. (Hear,hear.) He objected to an army composed of 90 or 95 per cent of working men being almost entirely officered by rich men, simply because they were the sons of their fathers. If they were to have an efficient army it must be open to com- petition, so that the son of the peasant as well as of the Prince should rise by his own merit and ability to the topmost rung of the ladder. (Cheers.)

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
ST. HELENS COLLIER INJURED.

Patrick Caveney, aged forty-four, a collier living at Fleet-lane, Parr, was admitted to the St. Helens Hospital on Saturday suffering from injuries to the back and head, caused by being crushed under a fall of roof at the Bold Colliery.

div.head: USING PADDY'S BRnASTPIN.
div.p: USING PADDY'S BRnASTPIN.

James Blakeley, of 4G, Hill's Moss-road,was convicted at St. Helens on Monday of an aggravated assault. The evidence was that on Saturday nigh the put the poker in the fire, and on his wife taking it out, he said, " Do you know what this is It is Paddy's breastpin." He then struck her a heavy blow on the left side of her head and felled her. He was sent to gaol for six weeks.

div.head: MOTORIST WETO DID NOT srop.
div.p: MOTORIST WETO DID NOT srop.

Mary Ellen Bratmon, a little girl, living at 8, Raven- head-passage, St. Helens, was crossing Liverpool-road, on Saturday evening, when she was knocked down by a motor-car which rendered her unconscious for two hours, and knocked out three of her teeth. The motorist drove on, it is said, without stopping to make an inquiry, but he has since been identified.

div.head: ST. HELENS MAN'S SEIZURE.
div.p: ST. HELENS MAN'S SEIZURE.

The man Joseph Ascroft, of 25, Havelock-street, St. Helens, who was seized with an apoplectic fit on Friday while repairing a roof near tvlessrs. Beecham's works, died on Saturday morning. Ascroft was fifty years of age, and weighed about 16 stone. After he was got down from the roof by the fire escape he was taken home, but never regained consciousness. The facts have been reported to the coroner.

div.head: INSOUNIA AND ATTENIPTED SUICIDE.
div.p: INSOUNIA AND ATTENIPTED SUICIDE.

James Burgess, glassmaker, of 7, Lewis-street, appeared at St. Helens on Monday, to answer a charge of attempted suicide. Mrs. Burgess said that on Saturday afternoon, March 23, Burgess went home and asked his wife what all the rumours were that were going about. Ho had been strange for some weeks, and could not sleep for a fortnight before. On the Saturday he was so strange that Mrs. Burgess went out to consult her sister about him. When she got back she found he had inflicted a wound six inches long in his throat, severing the windpipe. About Christmas he met with an accident and fractured his ribs, and he had never been right since. Other members of his family had been mentally affected. The Bench considered it would not,be safe to allow Burgess to go home. The relieving officer Ind better take him to the workhouse infirmary.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. BEECHAM.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. BEECHAM.

Mr. Thomas Beecham, the proprietor of the great pill manufactory at St. Helens, died at five o'clock on Saturday evening, at his residence in Southport. Mr. Beecham was eighty-six years of age. He was a native of Oxfordshire, and between fifty and sixty years ago started his commercial career as a chemist in Wigan, soon afterwards moving to St. Helens, where he built up the world-wide reputation of the business. Mr Beecham's career forms one of the pages of the romance of industry, and his name is quite as well known in America, Australia, India, and other parts of the world as it is at St. Helene. Phe business at St. Helens has for many years been under the charge of the deceased's son, Alderman Joseph Beecham, who some years ago was Mayor of the town. Mr.Beecham, sen., never took any active part in public affairs, but he regularly visited St. Helens, and was at , the works only about a fortnight ago. He had not ' been well for some time, but had been bedridden only a fortnight. Mr. Beecham commenced his business in St. Helens by opening a shop in Westfield-street, a few yards from the spot where, thirty years later, the present palatial manufactory was erected. He had not taken an active part in the business for over twenty years, so that the present generation in the town is not very familiar with his personality, but his name will always be sssociated with the early development of the town. Many striking incidents of his energy and business ability are still related by the earlier residents. The wonderful manner in which he built up his business with his genius for advertising was the admiration of everybody who knew him. Locally he was a veil- just man of business, prompt in his deal- ings, and a generous employer. He had a most unosten- tatious disposition, caring nothing for dress or display. He gave liberally to most of the deserving charitable objects of the locality, and contributed £5OO towards I rebuilding the St. Helens Congregational schools. The ' present factory was built in 1885, and the many beautiful works of art which it contains, with the original drawings and advertisements, make it the chief show place of the town. The business in America was established in 1888, and the firm have a large factory in New York.-- The deceased's two sons are Aldernaan Joseph Beecham, who now carries on the business, and Dr. William Beecham, of London. Both these gentlemen took an active part in founding the St. Helens Cyclists' Club, and were successful couipetit)rs in the club champion- ship races, which have always been most popular in- stitutions. The firm are said to be the chief newspaper advertisers in the world, and probably rank as the largest single advertising concern.ln one year they spent over £llO,OOO in advertising. In the various branches they employ about 150 people, and the volume of the exports even exceeds the consumption of the home market.

div.head: ' FUNERA L.
div.p: ' FUNERA L.

The funeral of Mr. Thomas Beecham took place on Wednesday afternoon at St. Helens Cemetery. In acnordance with the wishes of Mr. Beecham, the funeral was of a very quiet description, the time and place being almost kept a complete secret. The remains were conveyed by road from Southport, and the funeral service was conducted by the Rev. G. E. Cheeseman, of Huyton. The mourners were: Mr. William Beecham ( Warwick), brother of the deceased; Alderman J. Beecham and Dr. William Beecham, London (sons), Messrs. Harry Beecham and E. Pemberton (grandsons), Mr. Boston (Huyton), Mr. C. Rowed, Mr. H. S.. Oppenheim, Mr. Watkin Oppeuheim, Mr. Thomas West worth, sen., Mr. W. Moss, Mr. C. T. Scrymgeour, Mr, E. Glover, Mr. E. Bamford, Mr. A. Scott, Mr. E. Marsh Mr. J. Lightfoot, Mr. A. Atkinson, and Mr. B. Littler. The bearers were some of the oldest employees of the firm—Messrs. J. C. Allin, W. 'Ackary, T. Metcalfe, G. Oldham, E. Lowe and J. Parr. There were also present at the graveside a number of residents who had succeeded in discovering the time when the funeral would take place. At the service in the mortuary chapel the Rev. G. E. Cheeseman addressed th 3 assembly, and said they were net to pay their last tribute to a man who although widely known, was best understood as a St. Helens man.

div.head: Sale of Pedigree Hackneys.
div.p: Sale of Pedigree Hackneys.

Sir Gilbert Greehall, Bart. held his annual sale by auction of pedigree hackneys, at Walton Hall on Thursday. There was a large attendance when Mr. W. Bainbridge mounted the rostrum, and the bidding was brisk, some 43 lots and £2,230 changing hands. The highest price realized was 180 guineas, paid by Mr. Gemmel', Ayr, for Terrington Columbine, a yearling filley. Mr. Gemmel" was a large buyei, becoming the possessor of eight lots at an average price of GO guineas. Mr. Caleb Jones, Sheffield, pa'id 135 guineas for a pony mare foaled in 1901. The lowest price of the day was 18 guineas.

div.head: REV. THOMAS LAW SAILS FOR AMERICA.
div.p: REV. THOMAS LAW SAILS FOR AMERICA.

Rev. Thomas Law Secretary of the National Council of the Evangelical! Free Churches, left England for America on Tuesday. A large and enthusiastic crowd witnessed the departure of the s.s. Carmania from Liverpool. Mr. Law's fellow travellers wete Mr. Charles F. Aked and his family. During Mr. Law's stay in America he will address the Ministers and leaders in New York, Boston, Chicago, Pittsburg, Washington and Philadelphia. Among other engagements Mr. Law will attend the Peace Banquet over (which Mr. Carnegie will preside at which President R4osevelt, Mr. Bryce the English Ambassador, and other leading Senators and Mr. W. T. Stad will be present.

Mrs. Betty Brooks, of Edgehill, Worsley, who has lust attained her 94th birthday, has passed all her life in the same cottage, one of a row belonging to the Earl of Ellesmere, at Bdgefold, Worsley, near Manchester.

div.head: SETTLER'S LIFE IN CANADA.
div.p: A SETTLER'S LIFE IN CANADA.
Warrington's Man's Experiences.

Mr. Edwin Porritt, 757, Knutsford-road, has received an interesting letter from his son Mr. Wallace Porritt, who gives a graphic account of his experiences at Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, Canada. The writer says : This has been an awful winter—the longest and most severe spell of cold weather that has been known for twenty-five years. There has been about one train every week in Prince Albert up to about twelve days ago. Some of the lines will not be in working order Ifor several weeks or till the snow has gone. The people who came out last summer and late in the jseason and settled on the prairie were not half fixed up for the winter. I guess they had'nt any idea what the winters were like out here, and as the result they did'nt have a warm enough house. They had not half the amount of wood to last the winte; and a lot of them have suffered very much. Some of them have been fr lzen, land in some districts several families have got together in one house to make the wood last. In the Calgarry district, where so much ranching is done, the cattle suffered very much, and thousands are dead in the snow. Round Prince Albert and down as far as Regina is abiut the coldest place in the country. , West at Edmonton it isn't half as bad, and the winter is shorter. Lots of fellows in the lumber camp have had their hands or feet frozen. The Hospital and a house at the west end of the town have both been full. There is an old fellow boarding at the same house with me and all his fingers are frozen, so he is as helpless almost as a baby. He does not seem to have much money, and the town is paying his board. He is just out from Dublin about seven months.

There is going to be a lot of railway building out West this summer. The Canadian Northern Railway Company are building a bridge over the Hirer here; it will be a big job as the river is very wide. This next seasrm is going to be good. The brewery was burnt down last Monday—vats of beer' machinery, and nearly the whole outfit-31,000 dols.-damage with. , about 7,000 dais, insurance. Work is not very plenti- ful just now, except some jobs that I would not have. It has snowed a lot again and the train hasn't gone out to-day; the track is snowed up, after all the work that has been done to keep it open. People have been paying 5 dole. a cord for stove wood, 35 cents for butter, and in fact everything is correspond- ingly high. Rents are something awful —l2dols for any kind of a place just large enough to live in, one to two dollars a day for board in the hotels and from 11o1s a week in private boarding houses. I have been in some of the places for 4dols. and they are awfully, dirty, and ever so many in one room. lam now pav- ing 41do1s. and it is a fine place, clean and good food. The people are English. You see this is a bush town and the old timers, of whom there are so many, are the worst kind and think anything will do for a man as ' long as it is a shelter. You would be surprised if you , saw how some of these men live. You can see whisky and beer bottles in the corners and under the beds, and they don't half drink—finish a bottle of whisky in no time:

If some of the fellows out of offices &c., who come out here just knew what it was like they would'nt come, for generally they are no good for work in this country, and if they have a little when they come, someone soon gets hold of it in some way or other. When the Bar Colonists came out five years ago they had lots of money—they came by train as far as Saskatoon and walked or rode to Loydminster. They ' were persuaded to buy all kinds of machinery they did'nt want and they paid twice as much as the stuff was worth. Same of them paid as much as 360d015. for a yoke of oxen and there were plenty of horses that they could have bought for the same money. One can hardly believe that people would do such things. Some of the women were seen carrying dishes and all kinds of things. The men got their oxen fast in sloughs and when a person has seen the country it is only then that it is possible to imagine what a time they must have had. They even blught rapers to cut the wheat with and paid 150 dols. for them before they had ever seen the land! A person has to be in this country to see how the Englishman gets done and in every case almost it is fellows from London and the large cities who have never seen a plough or any farm work done who come off worst. Some of them go to the bush and get the " push" in about three days. When these Canadians want men they will promise any wage and when it comes to pay- ing it's another thing. What you used to tell me—that a person should come with no money —is about right, for nearly everyone that I know of lost it all one way or another. Mr. Porritt concludes his letter with a brief and technical description of lumbering.

div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

The members of this guild brought a successful session to a close on Saturday evening with a " social " which was held in the Lecture Hall. There was a large attendance and a thoroughly enjoyable evening was spent. An attractive musical programme was submitted a special feature being conclrtina solos by Mr. Ford who also acted as accompanist.

div.head: Bevisey-road Wesleyan Church.
div.p: Bevisey-road Wesleyan Church.

The annnal home missionary meeting in connection with this church was held on Thursday evening and was well attended. The Rev. E. J. Gawne delivered a most interesting address on his work among the soldiers at Port.mouth. Miss Lester gave an effective rendering of " 0 Divine Redeemer," and ft quartette from "The Holy City" was sung by members of the choir, Mr. E. Pearce taking the bass solo.

div.head: P.S.A. Meetings
div.p: P.S.A. Meetings

There was a good attendance at the meeting of the Wycliffe P.S.A.. on Sunday. The hon. secretary pre- sided. Mr. R.. Lewis read the lesson, and Mr. Payton presided at the organ, !qr. W. J. Barnes sang " Pray brethren pray "in a telling manner. In the Absence of the speaker who had missAd his train ast Nfanchester,gr. A. Healey spoke some timely words on "God's sparing mercies." div.head: Christ Church Vestry Meeting.
div.p: Christ Church Vestry Meeting.

The Rev. G. C. Briggs presided over the Easter vestry meeting in connection with Christ Church, Latchford. which was held on Saturday evening. Mr. John Fairclongh, in presenting the accounts, said they showed a deficit on the year's working of about £2O. Their expenditure had been £22S Os. lOd.. whereas their income had only been V. 117 18s. lid. They had brought forward a debit balance from the previous year of £22. _ _ _

Messrs. John Fairclough and W. Longbottom having intimated their desire to retire from office, the Vicar nominated Mr. I. T, Williams as his warden. Mr. W. J. Forshaw was unanimously elected people's warden. Mr. Williams nominated Mr. Whyman ns his sidesman, and Mr. Forshaw nominated Mr. R. T. Fairclough as people's sidesraan. The following were also elected to serve as sidesmen : —Messrs. George Dakin. Dutton. Fairclough, John Fairclough, W. Limb, W. Longhnt,tom, A. Lowe, J. Lowe, T. H. Plevin, W. Tinsley and G. Venn. Messrs. R. T. Fairclough and J. Lowe were re-elected as lay delegates. Mr. W. Longbottom was appointed auditor.

div.head: COUNTY COURT JUDGE AND ALLEGED
div.p: COUNTY COURT JUDGE AND ALLEGED
PERJURY.
Strong Comments.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, "tfessrs Gartons Ltd, seed merchants, Warrington. sued Thomas Poster, farmer, of Eastrington, Brough, Yorkshire. for £lO balance alleged to be due on account.. Mr. Browne represented the plaintiffs and defendant appeared in person. Mr. Browne said that in March 1904 plaintiffs' traveller,Mr. Jennings,took an order from defendant for five quarters of oats at 535. per quarter. The same night he sent on the order direct to the firm at Warrington. The five quarters of oats were dispatched and invoice sent to defendant. Sono time afterwards by an unfortunate .error of a typist a letter was dispatched by the firm asking for the payment of £4 103. instead of £l4s. 10s., to which the defendant did not reply. A subsequent letter was sent asking, plaintiffs alleged, for payment of £l4 103. Defendant, some months afterwards remitted the sum of £4 10s. awl a receipt was forwarded in due course. Another letter was sent to the defendant asking for the balance of £lO but he did not reply. Tne matter as placed in the solicitors' hands andigkey wrote in the usual way, but there was again no Mwer. The case was entered in the County Court and correspondence ensued between a firm of chartered accountants carrying on business in Goole. and Messrs. Arthrn Browne and Co., in which the accountants alleged that two letters written by the plaintiffs mentioned the sum of £4 10s. At the request of plaintiffs' solicitors one of the letters dated 13th August, 1905, was sent to Warrington for inspection, and on examination it was immediately found that the same had been tampered with and that in front of the £1 there had been a recent erasure. Such letters and erasure were taken particular notice of under a strong magnifying glass and returned to the accountants with notice'to produce the same at the trial. At the request of his Honour the defendant handed up the letter and his Honour, using the magnifying glass, at once said there was no shadow of doubt that the erasure was a recent one. _ _

Mr.- Brown 43 pointed out that Itessrs. Gartons had. never sold oats at snch a ridiculous sum as 18s. per quarter which defendant alleged was the amount agreed upon in as much as they cost the firm a great deal more than that to produce.

Witnesses baying been called for the plaintiffs, his Honour stopped the case and asked defendant what answer he had to give with regard to the erasure. Defendant denied tampering with the letter and declared that he bought the oats at 18s. per quarter and not at 565.
His Tionnnr painted out that plaintiff's catalogue showed that defendant's evidence was absurd.
Defendant was again pressed about the erasure but pArsisted in his statement that he had no knowledge of it.

His Honour said that the amount of perjury com- mitted in the County Courts since he had presided was enormous, and he was seriously thinking of giving into custody some persons for wilfully committing perjury. He had no hesitation in saying that he believed defend- ant had erased the" 1 " in front of the "4." He had a good mind to order him to be taken into custody for Perjury, but seeing that he was an old man and such a long way from home he would not do that. He advised defendant to be more careful in future, and gave a verdict for the plaintiffs for the amount claimed with costs. He ordered defendant's letters, Sco., to be impounded by the Court.

div.head: DEATH OF MRS. BERTHA MORGAN.
div.p: DEATH OF MRS. BERTHA MORGAN.

Many of our readers will regret to hear of the death, under particularly distressing circumstances, of Mrs. Bertha Morgan, which occurred at the residence of her mother, 46, Bewsey-street, on Tuesday morning. The deceased lady, who was the youngest daughter of the late Mr. Ralph Norman, for many years Inspector of Nuisances for the Borough, was only in September of last year married to the Rev. John Edward Morgan, curate of Llangollen Parish Church. She was well- known in Warrington, especially in St. Paul's parish in which she did good work as a Sunday school teacher. Death was due to consumption of the throat.

div.head: NEW THEOLOGY.
div.p: THE NEW THEOLOGY.
" Spiritual Champagne and Egg-Flip."

At the seventy-ninth conference of the Manchester and Liverpool District 'Primitive Methodist Ministerial Association, at Widnes on Wednesday, the Rev. J. Day, Thompson delivered an address entitled" Some impres- sions of the Rev. R. J. Campbell's book upon the New Theology." He said that the publication of the bookhad practically been forced upon Mr. Campbell, who was largely the child and creature of the atmos- phere in which he lived. Mr. Campbell was eager, ebullient, and excitable—a true Celt. He had the blood of Campbell clan in him, and be was a born fighter. He had now placed his hack to the wall, and sought to give an account of himself and his critics. His book was intensely alive, full of intelligence and vivacity. The speaker did not know that he would describe it as the ripe fruit of intellect. It was rather a ferment— not bread but yeast.—(Laughter.) But he would remind them that yeast was necessary for the production of bread. The book was a kind of intellectual and spiritual champagne. (Laughter.) Perhaps it was not milk for babes,l and perhaps not meat for strong men. It partorili of the character of that exquisite " egg- flip " which Mr. Gladstone used when he was making one of his magnificent speeches in the House of Commons.—(Laughter. It was a book full of insight and poetic cmice. The speaker was sorry for Dr. Robertson Nicol's criticism of it. He had lost confidence in Dr. Nicol as a leader in view of his treat- ment of Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman and the side he had taken in the London County Council election. (Applause.) He was sorry that Dr. Fairburn seemed to think that the position Mr. Csmpbell had won in the religious world and in Conzregationalism had been awarded him by favour. That was not so; be had fairly and honestly won it. (Applause.) Later, in the conrse of his address, the sneaker said that Mr. Campbell's theology might be safe for him' but it would not be safe for people of weak ethical instincts. Were it preached to men on gibbets, in brothels,and in gaol the result would be a very carnival of lust and crime.

Sammy broke suddenly into the parlour one day, and came upon his aunt Margaret. sit%ng on Mr. Brown's knee. The surprised couJie hastened to pull wool over the youngster's eyes. "We are rehearsing for a little play, Sammy," explained Aunt Margaret. "Yes. Samuel, added Mr. Brown, with a touch of sentiment in his voice; "I am now holding the queen." "You must be good at it," answered Sammy, as he backed out of the room; " I heard Uncle Jack say that you held four queens last night."

Professor John Stuart Blackie, of Edinburgh, being suddenly called away by an important summons one day, posted this notice on his classroom door for his students: " Professor Blackie will be unable to meet his 'classes to- day." Some waggish students came along and rubbed out the "c " from the word classes. The professor, reaching home that evening, saw the erasure, chuckled, and promptly erased the letter "L" His students ever afterward had great respect for their teacher!

An Irishman was walking along a road beside a golf links when he was suddenly struck be- tween the shoulders by a golf ball. The force of the blow almost knocked him down. When he recovered he observed a golfer running to- ward him. "Are you hurt?' asked the player. "Why didn't you get out of the way?" "An' why should I get out of the way?" asked Pat. "I didn't know there were any assassins round here." " But I called 'fore,'" said the player, "and when I say 'fore,' that is a 5;.;..n for you to get out of the way." " Oh, it is. is it?" said Pat.. "Well, thin, whin I say foive,' it is a sign that you are going to get hit on the nose. Foive.' "

I have written in former notes of the effect of railway rates on trade and agriculture but it is possible that the average man, who is neither a trader nor an agriculturalist, has not been particularly interested although it could easily be proved that railway rates, in affecting trade and agriculture, do indirectly affect most of the community. Almost every man and woman, however, now travels by train and if I can prove that they pay more for that privilege than the residents in France, Germany, or Austria, I shall have provided them with some food for thought. Well, here are some comparisons from Austria and Hungary. From London to Birmingham, a distance of 113 miles, the fare is Os. 5d., the same distance in Austria is 55., and in Hungary 6s. From London to Edinburgh, 400 miles, the fare is 335., in Austria it would be 16s. 3d. and in Hungary Bs.!

With respect to the all important question of work- man's trains the difference between the privately owned and managed English railways and the publicly owned and controlled railways of the Continent is just as great ; from a report by a Mr. Reid, of the London County Council, I quote the the following eloquent figures: where a workman in London spends 14s. id. in travelling to and from his work, the worker in Berlin spends Bs. 4d., in Paris 7s. 7d., in Brussels ss. 7d. in Vienna Bs. Thus we see how, on every hand, the worke. is taxed and bled by railway companies to-day.

div.head: ALL, CHANGE!
div.p: ALL, CHANGE!

There must be a remedy. There is. In all the countries of Europe and in Australia and New Zealand the majcr portion of the railway system is owned and worked by the people themselves and we shall never remove any of the evils I have mentioned until we
NATIONALIZE THE RAILWAYS

When we do that, and it can be done quite easily, we shall have railway rates sufficiently low to give British trade and agriculture a fair chance • we shall have fares low enough to enable our tilers to work in the town and live in the country and at holiday times and week-ends to get about and see the land they are so often told is their noble heritage ; we shall be able to lessen the danger to life and limb which are such a deplorable feature of railway work; and we shall be able to give the workers better hours and wages and fairer conditions of labour generally. Lastly, we shall be able to earn a sufficient profit to go a long way towards the provision of an old age pensions for all when we Nationalize the Railways. STANLEY LORD.

ENGLISH SWEATING, AND NOT YIDDISH. An inquest was held on Wednesday by Mr. Wynne E. Baxter, at Stepney, respecting the death of Harold Kight, aged twelve months. Florence Knight, the mother, a poorly dressed young woman, with a thin, haggard face, said her husband deserted her twelve months ago, a few days after the boy was born. There .were two other children, but only one was now alive. She was com- pelled to go out washing and charing to keep things going. The Coroner: How much do you earn ?—Some- times ss. a week, sometimes 65., but never more than 7s. Her mother, the witness added, looked after the child while she was away. As the result of a falla lump formed behind the child's ear. A doctor lanced it, but the next day the child seemed very ill, and she took him to the infirmary, where he died on Friday. Eliza Hales, whose appearance also denoted extreme poverty, said she was the wife of a shoemaker. On account of bad health he had not been able to do any work for some time, and was now an inmate of the infirmary. The Coroner: Then how have you lived ?—I have done trousers finishing. A juror: Does that pay well ? I have beard some- thing about it.—l get 2d. a pair.—(Sensation.) The Juror : I thought so. There's an existence! Do you have to find your own thread ?—Yel, sir— find everything. I have often worked until four o'clock in the morning to get a crust Al bread. ' (Sensation.) I have been paid 2-Id. a pair for heavy, lined trousers. The Foreman of the Jury: Splenaid ! And this is our beautiful, fine country ! Put it all dcma, Mr. Reporter. Don't be afraid to let the public know,and make a special note that this is English sweating, and not Yiddish. The Coroner (to the mother): Why don't you go into the workhouse ? The Mother : If I do that, I shall lose my work. It will mean worse starvation when I come outagain. The jury returned a verdict of death from natural causes, and declined to express any further opinion. Those who have read Sesame and Lilies "will doubtless remember what John Ruskin said concern- the question "Why should witness not go into the Workhouse ? " How he remarked that "the poor seem to have a prejudice against the Workhouse which the rich have not ; for of course everyone who takes a pension from the Government goes into the Workhouse on a grand scale; only the workhouses for the rich do not involve they idea of work. and should be called play houses. /But the iSoor like to die independently, it appears." What some of us eannot understand, however, is the fact that in Christian England the Churches will squabble about a "farrago of nonsense" (in the form of Biblical criticism) and will insist upon neglecting the commands of Jasus Christ. Somehow, they will forget that Jesus Christ came into the world to seek and to save the poor and the outcast, and that He never spent five minutes in teaching the people how to get to Heaven without the sacrifice of worldly goods and profit. We have heard Socialism denounced as selfishness, but we are quite sure that under Socialism such a sad state of affairs could not exist. Its traducers have yet much to learn.
JOHN WORKMAN.

NINA'S EASTER EGG.

MY DEAR NIECES AND NEPHEWS,— I was really quite surprised to-day t 9 find that Easter was right here. By the'time you read this letter it will have gone by a week or so *Therefore, it is too late to offer you my best wishes for a pleasant Eastertide; but I hope that you enjoyed it all the same. What with those delicious Chocolate Eggs and the Hot Cross Buns, I cannot imagine any relation of mine incapable of deriving some happiness at such a time. I know one thing ("and," as the old lady said, "that ain't two")— that if there had been Chocolate Eggs in my young days, I shouldn't have been very miser- able. I am very pleased to announce that my Easter Post-bag contains five applications for membership. Welcome to the five, and con- gratulate ourselves •that three of them are Nephews. This week I am cutting my letter down, as I have many contributions, which I am anxious to publish, •and which you will he equally anxious to read. The Prizes this week are awarded to Niece "May Blossom" for an original story, entitled "Nina's Easter Egg," and Hilda Henchcliffe for "The Travellers and the Bear."
Now I will finish for this week, and begin to look forward towards receiving a good pile of Solutions •to the Corner Puzzles. UNCLE NED. WELCOME TO
Reuben Riley, May Bonfield, Louis Heneb- cliffe, Amy Bentley, Leonard Allatt.

" URASHIMA." (Concluded.)

Then it suddenly flashed across Urashima's mind that the Sea-God's Palace beyond the waves, with its coral walls and its ruby fruits, and its dragons with tails of solid gold, must be part of fairyland, and that one day there was probably as long as a year in this world, so that his three years in the Sea-God's Palace had really been hundreds of years. Of course, there was- no use in staying at home, now that all his friends were dead and buried, and even the village had passed away. So ITraehima was in a great hurry to get back to his wife, the Dragon Princess, beyond the Idea. But which was the way? He couldn't find it, with no one to• show it to him. "Perhaps," thought. he, "if I open the box which she gave me I shall be able to find the way." So he disolAyed her orders not to open the box—or, perhaps, he forgot them, foolish boy that he was. Anyhow, he opened the box, and what do you think came out of it ON"othing but a white cloud, which floated away over the sea. Urashima shouted to the cloud to stop, rushed about and screamed with sorrow; for•he remembered now what his wife had told him, and how,- after opening the box, he should never be able to go to the Sea-God's Palace again. But soon he could neither run nor shout any more. Suddenly his hair grew as white as snow' his face got wrinkled, -and his back bent like that of a _very old man. Then his breath stopped short, and he fell. down dead on the beach.

Poor Ura.shima 1 He died because he had been foolish and disobedient. If only he had done as he was told he might have lived another thousand years. Wouldn't you like to go and see the Dragon Palace beyond the waves, where the Sea-God lives and rules as King over the dragons and the tortoises and the fishes, where the trees have emeralds for leaves and rubies for berries, where the fishes' tails are of silver and the dragons' tails all of solid gold?

, - "Ruth! Ruth! Oh! do come here; come and look, Ruth." Ruth Day put her picture-book away in haste, and ran to join her brother Teddy. "What is the matter, Teddy?" she asked, when at last she found him seated beside a big parcel. "Oh! look what Uncle Ned has sent us," he cried, jumping up, and clapping his hands. "How do you know Uncle Ned has sent it?" inquired Ruth. "Because he has written to mother, and he says in his letter that the parcel is for us," •answered Teddy. "Well, let us unpack it, and see what it is," cried Ruth, who was by now as excited as Teddy, and they set to work with a will. All at once there was a shout of joy—they had pulled and torn the covering off, and there, amidst fancy paper, in two separate boxes, lay two big silver eggs. Silver, did I say? Well, Teddy and Ruth soon discovered they were chocolate. On one of them wae written "Ruth," and on the other "Teddy." Just then Mrs. Day came into the room. "You have not been lorrg in unpacking your Uncle Ned'a present, children," she said, with a smile. "Mother, just look what he has sent us," cried Teddy, holding up his egg, which already had a large piece eaten out. "Well, don't eat them all at once, or you will be ill," answered their mother, adding, "I am going to see Nina Sky this afternoon; would you like to go with me?" "Oh 1 yes, mother," they both cried. In the afternoon they went to visit Nina Sky, who was a little girl and blind. 43.utit and Teddy told her -I)ouetheir Eastet Eggs, and when they haa ,one, Nina could do nothing but think abeett what they had told her, and kept wishing she, too, had a lovely egg like theirs. That night, when Nina's mother had helped her to bed, she was a long time before she fell asleep; but she did at last,and this is what she dreamt:—She was walking along a path, and at last she came to a wood. Of course, she could not see, but felt her way. She sat down to rest awhile, when all at once she felt some- one beside her. "Who is it?" she cried, for she knew it was a stranger. "It. is I, the Fairy Starlight," answered a silvery voice, "and I have come to comfort you. Why are you looking so troubled, child?" and Nina told her all about Teddy and Ruth's eggs. "Would you like one, too?" asked the Fairy. "Oh! I should love one, cried Nina, clasping her hands. "But, then," she cried, despairingly, "I should not be able to see it." "Let me see if I cannot make you happy," said Fairy Starlight, and she stepped up to Nina and kissed both her eyes. No sooner had she done so than Nina saw the sunshine, the birds, and the pretty little fairy beside her. She was not half as big as Nina, and she wore a long, white, mist-like robe; •her arms and feet were bare; and she had lovely long golden hair. "Now for your Easter Egg," she said, with a smile, and she waved her wand. Four large golden butterflies appeared, drawing a lovely chariot, and reposing in it was the biggest Easter Egg Nina had ever heard of. 411" Now, dear child, be happy," said the fairy, as she rolled the egg out of the chariot and placed it beside Nina. "Good-bye," and she kissed Nina once more; then, stepping into the empty chariot, she disappeared. Nina wakened with a start, and great was her disappointment when she found it was all a dream. Nina told her mother about her dream, but she only looked troubled, for they were poor, and she could not take Nina to a great doctor, for she never ceased to hope that Nina would some day be able to see. When Mrs. Day came, during the day, Nina repeated her wonderful dream. When she had finished, Mrs. Day was determined to do all in her power to realise Nina's dream. That night Mi. Day wrote to a specialist, who came and operated upon Nina's eyes, and she was restored her sight. When at last the bandages were removed from her eyes, the first thing she saw was a huge egg, almost as big as the one Fairy Starlight had given her in her dream. She turned to her mother, and asked, "Who brought this, mother dear? Was it a fairy, with long, fair hair?" she added, eagerly. " No, it was a fairy with dark hair, and I hear her at the door," and she went to let the visitor in, who was no other than Ruth Day. Oh! Ruth, I em so happy; it is wonderful to be able to see, and I can't help thinking about Fairy Starlight. My dream has come tree, only Cie fairy who brought the egg has dark hair instead of fair. Do you believe in fairies, Ruth?" she asked. "Yes," answered Ruth, gravely, as she kissed Nina again and again. After that, Ruth and Nina became fast friends, and were never tired of roaming in the woods in 'search of the

THE PICNIC. We had a picnic one fine day-- Baby and I and sister May. Ma said we could, because we were good, And nurse took us off to the wood. She spread the cloth and made the tea, And down we sat so merrily, With jam and cake and strawberry sweet— We never had a grander treat. But all at once a dog came by, And nearly made the baby cry; He was so rude, he tried to take From sister May her piece of cake. He barked, and growled, and jumped about, And all of us began to shout. "Poor thing is hungry," Nursy said; "We'll feed him_ with some milk and bread."
We took him home, And never more he's going to roam. We call him "Little Picnic Tim," And now we're very fcmd of him.

Strict watch was kept at the local cemetery, and the next morning the man in question was observed making his way towards the cemetery. A razor WA4 found in his possession, and he was induced to go to the workhouse.

At prest about half thc? coke in Germany is prcd!3ffd in the 0h1.3v 6tyle of ovens which burn all their own gas.. and from which only exhaust heat is available for 'steam genera- tion. The other half of the cake, says the Engineering Magazine, is made in by-pro- duct ovens, where the gases are cooled and deprived of their tar, ammonia, benzol, &c.. and are then Used partly for heating the ovens therns•llves and for generating steam surnly

oeing available for as engi2es. By constructing these by-product ovens on the regenerative principle, all their gas can be used in gas engines. It has been esti- mated that the gas and waste heat • from the coke ovens in Germany are capable of pro- ducing from 500,000 to 600,000 horse-power, according aä they are used for steam genera- tion or in gas en,nnes, or partly for one and partly for, the (idler. Coke-oven-gas engines with -a total capacity- of 14,000 horse-power were actually in use, or in course of con- struction last summer.

Blast-furnace gas is a still more important source of power. With a monthly output of 1,000,000 tons of iron, which was slightly ex- ceeded by the blast furnaces of Germany in 1906, it is found that they generate enough gas to produce 1,000.000 horse-power if used in gas engines. or about half that amount if burnt under boilers in connection with the best reciprocating engines or steam turbines, and only oice-third of a million horse-power, or less, if used with steam engines such as are often found at metallurgical works and mines. The blast-furnace gas engine has made rapid progress, and in May, 1906, there were in operation or in course of construction in Germany such engines with a total cap- acity of 372,000 horse-power.

div.head: RADIUM IN MEDICAL SCIENCE.
div.p: RADIUM IN MEDICAL SCIENCE.

The Hospital points out that radium pos- sesses therapeutic properties, of considerable value.. Regarding its. physiological effects, radium penetrates the skin, and is capable of producing sloughing. For therapeutic pur- poses radium is enclosed in small capsules of thin glass, or in a box having a mica window in the centre. Special celluloid films, metal discs, and pencils can also be obtained coated with radium. The dose of radium is regu- lated by several factors: (1) The radio-ac- tivity of the salt used; (2) the weight of the salt; (3) the density of the part treated; (4) the thickness of the capsule enclosing the radium; and (5) the duration of the ex- posure. No pain or sense of heat is felt during the application. No authentic case of the successful curative action of radium on canoer has been reported. The various methods employed have produced no really stable results, apparently because they failed to attack the growth over the whole of its surface at the same time. • In dermatological practice radium, either alone or in combina- tion with the Finsen treatment, has been used successfully in lupus vulgaris. It is es- pecially useful in treating this disease in the nose, mouth, or other places where the light treatment can be applied. Capillary nwvi are very amenable to applications of radium, the smaller ones quickly clearing up, but the larger ones requiring time. A suitable method of treatment in skin affection is to cover the surface with cotton-wool made radio-active. Gelatine charged with radium emanations and spread on any suitable material acts perhaps better, as it retains the radio-activity for a longer period.

div.head: POISON OF THE UPAS.
div.p: THE POISON OF THE UPAS.

The upas tree has long been a familiar and picturesque legend in natural- history. And the fame of the upas arose through an article in the London, Magazine, December, 1783, purporting to be by'Foersch, who was sur- geon at Samarang in 1773. Erasmus Darwin. popularised the legend of the upas tree in his "Loves of the Plants," and it has scarcely yet ceased to flourish. For to this day it is still a common belief that birds fly- ing over it are poisoned, and that it is fatal to men and beasts resting beneath it. The rcal facto arc thut the tree emits a volatile substance, which affects people with very sensitive skins.

From the sap, again, the Dyaks of Borneo get the poison for their arrows. To obtain it the bark of the tree is cut, and the milky juice collected on a palm leaf. It is first of all dried in the sun, and then over the fire, when it becomes a thick brown mass. In this state it keeps a long- time. When required for use, it is made into a thin paste with the juice of the " tuba " root, or with tobacco or lemon juice. The arrows are made of the middle stem of the palm leaf, and are from Gin. to Bin. long, and of the thickness of a knitting needle. These being tipped with the poison are shot from a wooden blowpipe known as a sumpitan. This is 7ft. or Bft. long, and a • quarter -of an inch in diameter. A bird hit with a. poisoned arrow is killed in- stantly, and a pig dies in twenty minutes. Mell. Pelletier and Caventon isolated an active principle from the upas poison, which they named antiarin, Antiaris toxicaria being the name of the tree. Another species, Upas- tiente, a climbing plant, furnishes an arrow poison even more effective than the ordinary upas tree. Borneo and the islands of the East Indies are the native country of the upas. The first-named upas belongs to the Artoearpus section of the great nettle order, while the latter is botanically Strychnos Tieute, and belongs to the Logania family.

div.head: WASPS AND THEIR WAYS.
div.p: WASPS AND THEIR WAYS.

Many are the lessons which the observer may learn from wasps, according to Dr. Dal- linger, who has been studying their habits, nesting methods, surgical skill, architectural ability, and, last) but not least, their social customs for upwards of forty years. "Wasps," said Dr. Dallinger, at a recent lecture, " are, highly social, or they are soli- tary." The average 'nest contains as 'many as 30,000 individual wasps, the whole struc- ture being built with the utmost ingenuity and skill, despite the apparently discourag- ing fact that it serves only for a single season. The early sunshine starts the wasp queen into action; she proceeds to find a suitable building site in a tree or branch, and enters in earnest on her. work of

div.head: CONSTRUCTING THE FAIRY CITY
div.p: CONSTRUCTING THE FAIRY CITY

to accommodate the myriads of busy insects. Early wasps are hatched out as workers, and as the wasp queen goes on gluing On more eggs into the cells the number of Workers rapidly.. increases. The workers are employed in the search for building material, and the nest is continually enlarged as occasion de- mands. The temperature of the nest is hif,h,. for without plenty of warmth, said Dr. D'al- linger, wasps cannot thrive or live. . Wasps are divided into. three elasscs—tie queens, the males or .drones, and the workers. The drones, it is interesting to note—as with bees.-----do not sting. They scarcely deserve the name applied' to them, for they have im- portant duties to perform,.. in that they act

div.head: SCAVENGERS AND SANITARY INSPECTORS
div.p: SCAVENGERS AND SANITARY INSPECTORS

for the wasp city. The wasp queen rules over the city, inside which the most perfect harmony prevails. "it is on the rarest oc casions that the peace is disturbed," said the lecturer, "and even when conflict takes place it is not deadly in its effect." The govern- ment is such that everyone enjoys perfect liberty, though none is allowed to become a burden to the state. If the queen is des- troyed the other wasps still continue to pursue their work with undiminished energy. Cold and wet are the deadly enemies of asps. Another species of wasp build tiftir nests in the ground. Their habits, however, differ very little from those of the tree wasps. The ground wasps are abundantly provided with the means of excavating in the earth. Refer- ring to hornets, Dr. Dellinger pointed out that their sting is very powerful. Their building material is nearly the same as the wasp, with the exception that it is coarser. In conclusion; the lecturer quoted instances which went to show that wasps are not alto- Fether devoid ot reasoning power, aaning the wasp is not merely a creature with a sting, but a creature with at least the traceS of a mind.'t

div.p: ST. PAKT, SALE OF WORK.
EJcce,ssial Aanual

The annual sale of work in connection with St. Paul's Church attracted a large and fashionable attendance to the Conservative Club Assembly Room on Monday, and the proceedings were in every way successful. The Rev. W. Bracecaron presided over the opening ceremony which was performed by Niiss Markel. The CHAtumAN at the outset eNpl4ined that during the past year they had built a now vestry nnd ri-novated their Chtuch at a cost of about Zl,OOO and they were anxious to pay off the debt .2400 which still remained. They werenot a rich congregation but they did their best and tried to help themselves and believed that was why, in the past, outside friends had helped them so liberally. He was pleased to welcome Miss Markel. (Applause.) Dr. Markel was well-known and every- thing he did was well done and he had the good of the town at heart. A progressive man, Dr. Markel did his best for the town and, he was glad to say, for St. Paul's las well. (Applause.) Miss MARKEL then gracefully performed the cere- mony allotted to her, wishing the sale every success. Mr. J. H. SMETHURST proposed a vote of thanks to Miss Markel for her services. He knew from experience of the great and practical interest which. Dr. Markel took in St. Paul's. (Applause.) As they would be aware at St. Paula they had the poorest 'endowment in the town and therefore it was essential that there annual sale should be a success. Whilst they tried to help themselves they were ever ready to help others as the position they occupied in the list of Hospital Sunday collections would show. (Hear, hear.) Mr. RIGBY seconded and the Rev.E. Peters supported the vote which was heartily accorded, Dr. Maikel briefly responding. The stalls which bore a large variety of articles attractively displayed, were in charge of the following ladies :—G. F. S. stall, Mrs. Cox and Miss Pickton ; Bible class stall, Mrs. Robinson and Mrs. Binks ; ladies work stall, Mrs. Gibson Smith, Mrs. Lord, Mrs. Worrell and Miss D. Reid; Miss Geddes stall, Mrs. Hepherd, Mrs. Westwell and Miss H. Burgess; competi- tion stall, Miss Sherwin; vicarage stall, Mesdames Bra cecamp, Lindley, T. Locker' Jolley, Smith, and Miss Walsh ; refreshment stall, Mesdames Beesley White, Laughtou, Bunch, Powis, Misses Wainwright, Gittens, Houghton and Smethurst; flower stall, Mes- dames Rigby, Young, Collin, Ayer, Misses Collin and Greenough' tea stall. Misses Finney and Fowler; sweet stall, Misses W. Bracecamp and A. Kenyon. The proceeds of the sale amounted to £295.

div.head: " Guardian" Conversion.
div.p: The " Guardian" Conversion.

Sir,—The fact that the local brewers and the local Tory leaders have together purchased the " Guardian " is of very portentous import to this district, and a further indication that the Conservative cause (includ- ing the Church ard Religious Education) is to be locally carried on the top of the beer barrel ! I say a further indication because we saw the first step taken at the annual meeting of the local Conservative Associa- tion when the head of one of our two local breweries was made President, and the local representative of the other, Vice-Chairman of the party. The identical names are prominent in the new directorate of the "Guardian." Surely the forces of human and political prop Tess, and of temperance and genuine religion will awake and join issue with this unholy alliance ?—Yours Sze., L IBA.

Sir,—l was much interested in reading your short article last week with reference to the change in the proprietary of the " Guardian " newspaper. It does indeed seem significant that so strong a combination of local gentlemen who are closely identified with the Conservative party or the brewing interest, or both, should have Obtained control of the " Guardian " at a juncture when licensing monopolies are seriously threatened and Toryism is fighting for its very existence against Liberal and Labour coalition. What it means I don't know, but time will tell. In connection with these seven gentlemen you mention there is another coincidence which you appear to have overlooked.lf I am not mistaken all are members or supporters of the Established Church. This is surely a fact also worthy of note, in connection with a r.te.ws- paper professing neutrality "in all matters political and religious." However difficult it has been in the past for the "Guardian" to avoid a bias, the difficulty must be intensified with such a heavy top-weight.. I sympathise with those who have •to guideits policy along a path at all times beset with difficulties.—Yours truly.
NEUTER.

div.head: Free Churches and the Congo. Letter from the President of the National
div.p: The Free Churches and the Congo. Letter from the President of the National
Council.

Sir,—At the National Convention of Free Churches in Leeds last March, it was resolved that "an appeal should be made to every Free Church in the land and to every conference and other assembly of organised Free Churches to lay on the conscience of their members, and on all whom they can influence the Christian duty of using every effort to secure for the natives of the Congo Free State deliverance from the wrongs insepar- able from the present system of administration, for which our own Government has so great moral respon- sibility." In accordance with this resolution we have advised that the Congo Misrule should be made the subject of special prayers and addresses on Sunday next, the 14th of April. The atrocious misgovernment and oppression in the Congo Free State, reported by Christian Missionaries, attested by a British Agent, confirmed by a Belgian Commission are now matter of common knowledge. And with this common knowledge (which has long been eating the heart of those who were within the circle of recognised facts) there has arisen throughout the country a demand for a common action, which may free the oppressed from devestating tyranny, and the nations who are respon- sible for establishing King Leopold's rule on the Congo from an overwhelming moral burden. As Sir Edward Gray say* "We cannot wait for ever." The administration of the Congo Free State has resulted in a system of forced labour worse than slavery and accompanied by the grossest outrages, murders and cannibalism, a system which throttles trade, turns the idea of human progress into a hideous caricature, and makes the situation a scandal of the world. Grave responsibility for the continuance of this terrible state of things must rest on England, as on the other States which were parties to the Berlin Convention. And we appeal to the Christians of England to press on the Government the duty and the urgency of using all the rights and all the powers which they ,possess to bring the oppression and cruelties which have been suffered too ion,' to an immediate end. In the hope that you will enlist the sympathies of your people with this great cause,and lead their prayers to His throne, Whose ears are open to the cry of the distressed, and Who holds in His hands the hearts of Kings.-.-I remain; etc., - -
J. RENDEL HARRIS, President, National Free Church Council.

div.head: State Church.
div.p: A State Church.

Sir,—A State Church may be properly described as a human institution formed by the union of a religion, not necessarily the best, with the secular power for the advantage of both in many ways. The story of the origin and development of the institution in England may not be without interest even now after a long interval of fourteen hundred years. In the sixth century Gregory, surnamed the Great, before he became Pope was one day walking in the forum at Rome, when he saw a number of handsome boys exposed for sale. The spectacle moved his com- passionate heart and learning that they were heathens, and came from the Island of Britain he then and there formed a resolve that that distant province of the Empire should, sooner or later, be won over to the faith. Nor did the somewhat troubled state of the times in whith he lived divert him from his purpose. For as soon as possible after his elevation to the Papal chair he sent Augustine, provost of his monastery at Rome, accompanied by forty monks, to carry out his noble design. The little party landed at Ebbesfleet in the Isle of Thanet in the year A.D. 597. Ethelbert, a Dane, was then the King of Kent, and hearing of the arrival of the Missionaries he proceeded to the shore where he was met by Augustine and his monks bearing a silver cross and a picture of our Lord on a board, and singing litanies for the conversion of the King and his people. The mission appears to have prospered, for it is related that at the first Christmas festival Ethelhert himself and ten thousand of his subjects were baptised in the channel which divides the island of Sheppey from the mainland. Indeed so pleased was the King with Augustine and his work that he gavel up to him his own palace at Canterbury and lands and possessions to found and supp4rt a See. And thus through the instrumentality of a converted Danish Prince and a few Italian priests was set up the State Church of England nhich for more than nine centuries continued to use the Roman ritual and to acknowledge the Pope's supremacy. Early in the sixteenth century, however, a new state of affairs arose. Henry the WIT. having quarrelled with Rome about the divorcement of one of his wives, threw off his allegiance to the Pontiff, and a complaisant Parliament set him up as head of the Church. Other changes both civil and religious followed, and from that time, commonly called the Reformation period the State Church of England has been distinguished for its free circulation of the Bible, and for more liberty in its interpretation, while still retaining some of the dogmas and usages of Rome, including the human head- ship of the Church in the person of the Sovereign. Considered from a worldly point of view, such a Church might be admissible and free from injustice in a land where the people were all agreed upon a common form of worship ; but in this country we have outlived such a state of things by many ages. And to-day the Christianity of England is split up into a number of large and powerful divisions all differing from one another, and 911 claiming to be Churches of Christ. The maintenance by the Government of one of these divisions, perhaps not even the purest or largest, in a position of privilege and preference denied to tile others is, therefore, both unwise and invidious, and involves Ft a serious infraction of the Law of Christ which com- mands his followers to do unto others as they would have others do unto them. _ _

But this is not the only objection that can be urged against the State Church.; two more important reasons for dissent remain to be discussed. In the first place, there is no Divine authority for the institution. Jesus Christ, the founder of the Church, should be the only Exemplar in this and all other matters pertaining to the Christian religion. And it is a fact that neither by example nor by precept did he teach the doctrine of the Union of Church and State. And the reason is evident. His Gospel was the power of God unto salvation, and needed no human crutches for support. This explains why he avoided the Roman authority and the Jewish', Sanhedrim in the planting of His Church. His immedi- ate followers, the Apostles, in the first century,preached the same Gospel, and the little comronnities, both Jews and Gentiles, that were obedient to the faith through their instrumentality never heard anything from their lips about State patronage and control. Moreover, the 'New Testament Scriptures which are supposed to con- tain an authentic, divinely inspired and full record of the principles and polity of Christianity never make the slightest allusion to such a state of things. And in very , early times oven when Christianity had become greatly correlated by the world, the headship of the Church by a man or a woman was unknown. But in the fourth century the Emperor Constant set up the institution of Church and State, and since then it has been a standing disfiguration of the religion of Christ in most of the civilised countries of the world. The other objection to which I have referred is the pretension of the State Bishops to be successors of tho Apostles. This claim, even from a social point of view, is so transparently absurd and unjustifiable that one may well wonder how It is that intelligent men can be i found to endorse it. It s well known that most of the Apostles were humble fishermen who had left their nets and their ship on the Sea of Galilee to follow a Master who had nothing to offer them but a hope of glory in His coming Kingdom as a reward for t7hhesepeolyoevertlyy and t suffering His services would involve. divinly honoured men of Galilee,following the example sof their heavenly Master, bore no earthly titles or dis-

tinctions, but were known to their "little flocks" and : to the world by the simple names given to them by their parents. On the other hand, their would-be successors are lordly ecclesiastics who sit on thrones, i live n palaces, enjoy large revenues, and exercise no small share in ate politics and government of the country. Nor are they distinguished for the humility of the Apostles. Not only are they lords, but , they claim to be right reverend, very reverend and most reverend fathers in God, apparently In direct opposition to the toaching of Jesus in Matthew xxiii. 7,8, 9. Again, we know that the Apostles were endowed with supernatural powers, and could speak in all languages and perform miracles. But even Churchmen will, I think, hesitate to believe that their pretended followers have the gift of tongues and the power of healing. And finally, so much in bondage is the State Church to the State that even in the matter of" the laying on of hands," which was a special privi- lege of the Apostles, the Bishops appear to be merely the agents of the Sovereign. When the occupier of a See dies the King appoints his successor, but graciously commands the Bishops to consecrate the favoured man to his office. And this prefunctory ceremony is sup- posed to make the new prelate a successor of the Apostles !—Yours truly, lONA. April, 1907.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist."]

All Warringtonians expect to see the Warrington team in the final for the Northern Union Cup at five o'clock to-night. This may look like taking no account i of the opposition, but it s certainly expected that Swinton will have to bow the knee on the Wigan enclosure. There is a difference in class between the teams, and in weight too, which should tell in War- rington's favour. They have certainly no fear of the Lions in this encounter, and should, in my opinion,win the semi-final pretty comfortably.

In League engagements this season each team won on its own ground. At Warrington the score was 29-0 in favour of the homesters, while at Swinton, the Lions won by 8-3 after a hard game on a very bad ground. On that occasion both the Swinton tries were the result of Warrington's fumbling near the line, but on the whole Swinton adopted thetrselves much better to the conditions. A dry day and firm turf suit Warrington much better, and the men are hoping for such conditions this afternoon. The only meeting between Swinton and Warrington in cup-ties that I can recollect was the one in 1901 when Warrinton made a pointless draw at the colliery village and won the replay by 20 points to nil. That was the year they reached the final for the second time and finally suc- cumbed to Halifax. It is expected that Swinton will again prove a stepping stone to the final round.
The records of the two teams in this season's cup tournament are as follows :

Unfortunately Warrington will not be able to place their best team in the field, for Brooks and Jenkins each require another week before they will have recovered frcm their injuries. The substitutes will be Jordan and Hockenhall who, at any rate, should prove of equal calibre to anything on the other side. The rest of the men had been training carefully and benefited much from the brine baths at Northwich. Fish has been taken special care of at Longford and as the result of hard training he is in better condition than seemed possible. It was staying power which helped Warrington to win at Huddersfield, and the men should be fully equal to any demands on their physique to-day.
The selected side is : Tilley, full back ; Fish, Isherwood, Taylor and Jordan, threequarters ; 'Lees and Hockenhall, half backs ; Thomas, Boardman, Harmer, Belton, Heath and Shugars, forwards.

Swinton are fortunate in being able to put their best team in the field. Fielding was the only doubt- ful starter and he is reported to have recovered from the injury to his arm. The players have all been training at home and are reported to be in the pink of condition:

The Swinton team will be : Fielding, full back; Griffin, Wallwork, A. Valentine and Jones, three- quarters ; Booth and Cowell, half backs ; Simister (captain), Barnett, Lloyd, Hobson, Pomfret and D. Davies forwards.

The other semi-final is at Rochdale, where a very keen struggle between Oldham and Salford seems certain. Many critics are backing Salford for this match, but I shall be surprised if Oldham do not prove themselves just the better side.
The League semi-finals on Saturday resulted as expected, Halifax and Oldham beating Keiribley and Runcorn. The two former will play off for the championship at Huddersfield on Saturday next.
