The athletic club formed by the employees of Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Co. have acquired the ground in Lovely-lane which has long been used by the Sankey Wire Mills Club and have also rented the bowling green. The opening ceremony took place on Saturday but the weather was not favourable. However, both the pitch and the green were duly used and the members of the club are hoping to spend many pleasant after- noons on the grounds which they had been fortunate enough to secure.

Sankey Wire Mills have bad to look out for fresh quarters and at the annual meeting this week it was decided to rent a field in Longshaw-lane off Folly-lane. The club is in a very flourishing condition and it is hoped that the change of ground will not result in any diminution of the public support which it has enjoyed for so manyyears.

have bought a Park of fifty acres—dirt cheap, in my opinion—acquired Queen's Gardens and other open spaces, built a new Police Court which even its bitterest opponents call a " Palace" of Justice—(laughter)— erected a splendid Secondary School and Technical Institute, and built an Elementary School which the Government Inspector told me only yesterday was admirable, and was about the best he had seen. In addition to this we have acquired the Waterworks, and made them equal to the increasing needs of this increasing area, and saved Lord Avebury and his friends from any risks of lighting our shops and works and houses or running our tramways at a loss. Finally, 1 may again
A REMIND THE " BOGEYMEN "

who are continually seeking to scare us by drawing awful pictures of our ruinous municipal debt that, a year ago, our municipal assets amounted to not less than £1,692,867 and exceeded our liabilities by £429,609 a total surplus of over £6 per head for every man, woman and child in Warrington. If anybody says that such things as sewers are unrealizable assets, I reply that you can no more run a town without them than you can run a railway without its permanent way, or a canal without its water; that much, if not most of the property included in the balance sheet could probably be sold at a handsome profit; and that five, at least, of our main assets (the gas, water, electricity and tramway undertakings, and the markets, which account for something like a million pounds,) contrived, last year, in spite of the sins of our officials, and the impos- sibility of making municipal trading pay,to earn a gross profit of not less than t 55,916, which is enough to pay a dividend of 5 per cent. upon a sum of not less than £1,118,320. Of course, unlike most public companies, we apply a large share of this in automatically paying off our debt (I wonder how many of them would pay a satisfactory dividend under similar conditions) ; but, after paying sinking fund and interest and maintaining all our plant in proper order, we received from the Gas and narkets Committees alone, last year, in direct relief of the rates, not less than £16,382. which is equi- valent to a reduction of more than Is. 7d. in the 2, and is the largest amount received from these and similar sources of any town in England with the exception of Mr. Hallaway's famous old city of Carlisle. I will merely add that both the electricity and tramways departments are now making substantial profit, and,that in spite of the enormous expenditure upon extensions, we have good reason to hope that thell waterworks will soon once more begin to show a satisfactory balance. So that, gentlemen, I want you all to face the future with becoming cheerfulness. The Council, which has been of late so much denounced, has not served the borough badly after all, and if my friends

div.head: Works Competition.
div.p: The Works Competition.

Monday will witness the conclusion of the seconp stage in connection with the Warrington Works Com- petition. The second round this week has attracted large gates, which is particularly gratifying in face of the fact that the proceeds are in aid of local charities. The results of the week's matches are somewhat sur- prising, the majority of the teams winning with ease, and some close fights can consequently be expected in the succeeding stages. The games played were : Crosfleld's' 23 v Stockton Heath, 3 ; London and North- Western, 8 v St. Helens Cable, 5 • Wilderspool, 23 v Corporation, 3; Rylands, 30 v Orford Tannery, 0; Whitecross, 31 v Monks Hall, 0; Castle Rubber, 14 v Edelstens 0; Fletcher Russell, 5 Richmonds, 5. The draw for the third round, which commences on Tuesday, resulted as follows: Wilderspool V. Castle Rubber; Walker's or Wyman's v. Whitecross ; Fletcher's,.or Richmonds v.L. and N.-W.; Crosfi.elds' v. Rylands'.

Cycling. Saturday was a most disappointing day far the open- rig of the Warrington Cycling Club's season, rain]fall- ing heavily all .afternoon. Consequently, the majority of the members made the journey to Acton 'Bridge by train. A few of the hardier spirits, however, braved the elements, and cycled out, whilst a motor party apparently suffered little inconvenience from the weather. Mr. Dallow (an old Warringtonian) provided an excellent tea for the 30 members present, and a con- cert was afterwards held.
To-day's run is to Hunt's Cross 'via Woolton. Light- ing-tip time 8.6.

Bowling. The green at the Sankey-street Conservative Club is in first class condition and play will commence this aferneon, with a four-handed main for a number of valuable prizes presented by the committee. Matches are in course of arrangement with a number of clubs, and everything points a very successful season. A strong committee has been appointed, consisting of Mr. John Wells (chairman), Mr. Chas. Holland (vice-chairman), and Messrs. J. P. Taylor, J. H. Turner, J. Lockett, H. Thornton, S. Caldwell, R. Sewell, F. Turner, S. Grant, F. Aukland, J. Holland, F. Rutter, and W. J. Wilson (hon. secretary.)

div.head: TRADES EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.
div.p: TRADES EXHIBITION AT THE PARR HALL.
Modern Enterprise.

In these enterprising days manufacturers are ever on the alert to discover fresh means of bringing their products prominently before the public notice. One of the most popular and successful methods is the trades exhibition and the Parr Halt is at present the scene of a particularly attractive display of this kind organized by a syndicate of leading firms. Since the opening on Tuesday afternoon the hall has been thronged with visitors, and as the exhibition will con- tinue until Friday next opportunities are afforded to everyone to inspect it. The stalls are admirably arranged and in addition to tempting specimens of foods, there are numerous exhibits of labour-saving appliances which attract general attention. Sampling and tasting stalls are, of course, popular and everything possible is done to cater for the comfort and enter- tainment of the public. The following well-known firms are members of the syndicate and are the prin- cipal exhibitors . - Alfred Bird and Sons, Limited, Bird's custard powder and other home specialities; George Bray and Co., Limited, gas burners, mantles and gas lighting appliances; Cadbury Bros., Limited, who dispense samples of cocoa essence and chocolate; Chivers and Sons,Limited, jams, marmalade and table delicacies ; Hovis, who exhibit samples of the famous bread of that name ; J. Mackintosh, Limited, extra cream toffee ' • The " Matchless " Metal Polish Co., Limited, metal polish, &c.; The Nugget Polish Co., Limited, boot polishes and leather preservatives; A. and F. Pears, Ltd., toilet soaps and perfumes; Orme Evans and Co., Limited, gas cookers and fires, &c. The stands of several local exhibitors are of special interest. One of the first to attract attention is that of Wadworths which occupies the entrance hall. This enterprising firm shows a splendid collection of pianos, the Broadwood's being particularly well to the fore. It is unnecessary to enlarge upon the reputation of these instruments, for all who have heard a Broadwood must have been impressed with its excellence of tone. The little pamphlets relating to " Adventures of the Broadwood Piano" and "The Making of a Broadwood Pianoforte," are very interOsting. Wadsworths are also agents for several other noted makes of pianos. Mr. W. Thompson,of Knutsford-road, has a tempting show of Japanese goods, paintings, and post cards, and he has taken over the agency for the Finbat Kites. Coopers, of the Electric Studios, opposite Central Station, have an interesting exhibit of photographs. There are many entertainments and "side shows 't which / have been largely patronized. The Crescenl Ladies' Orchestra give capital concerts in the large hale at intervals, and in the evening the programme i rendered additionally acceptable by vocal selections by Miss Lily Fairhurst, Miss Woodland, and Mr. R. A. Robinson. In one of the ante-rooms biographical dis- plays are provided, and character delineations by Madame Hadley add to the interest of the exhibition. A feature which is welcomed by the ladies is a series of cookery lectures by an expert. The exhibition is under the capable management of Mr. H. Spencer Williams.

div.head: RATES REDUCED.
div.p: RATES REDUCED.
ALDERMAN BENNETT'S BUDGET SPEECH.
Municipal Trading Defended.

The welcome announcement that the rates of the borough would be reduced by 4d. in the 2, making the total amount 75.. was made at the meeting of the War- rington Town Council on Tuesday evening. The esti- mates were submitted, showing that the following amounts would be required. in respect of the various funds :—On the Borough rate,239,351 7s. 11. d.; Improve- ment rate, £26,825 13s. 7d.; General Sewers rate, £1,207 75.; total, £67,334 Bs. 6d. For the last four years the corresponding figures were : April, 1903.
April, April, April, 1904. 1905. -190 G.

ALDERMAN BENNETT'S SPEECH'. REPLY TO " JEREMIAHS " AND "BOGEYMEN." Alderman BENNETT, in submitting the budget,said : I much regret that owing to continued ill-health, the Chairman of my committee is unable to submit to you the Budget for the current year, and, that,in his absence this responsible duty devolves, for the first time, on me. lam sure that lam expressing your unanimous wish when I say that we deeply sympathize with Ar. Alder- man Fairclough upon his Indisposition, and earnestly hope that he may soon be back in the old place he filled with so much common sense and business shrewdness. I will give you, first of all, a brief resume of the results of the past year's working, and then explain how the rates we now propose to ask for are arrived at, resorv- ing any wider and more general reflections on the financial position of the town until a later stage in my remarks. Commencing with

THE BOROUGH RATE, I may say that there is a balance due to the bank of £1,120 14s. 7d. Ido not propose to trouble you by going through the figures in detail, and trust lam safe in assuming that you have all carefully studied them yourselves. But lam glad to be able to announce that the Town Hall,. Parks and Baths, Cemetery, Finance, Rivers and Watch Committees have kept within their estimates. The General Purposes Committee have exceeded theirs by £1,656, mainly in consequerfce of the Ship Canal action, the dispute with Colonel Edelsten, the experimental borings in connection with the scheme for widening Warrington Bridge; and the Gymnasium Committee, although underspent by .C4O, have not real- ized their expected income by £l36,owing to the change which has been made in the arrangements with the Education Committee. To turn to

div.head: IMPROVEMENT RATE.
div.p: THE IMPROVEMENT RATE.

Here we have a balance in hand of not less than :22,786 Gs. sd. The finance, fire engine, health, sanitary works, markets, street improvement, and scavenging depart- ments have all kept within their estimates, and I note with satisfaction, a growing desire on the part of practically all the committees to cut their coats accord- ing to then. cloth. The only departments which come out on the wrong side are the Weights and Measures and the Highway Departments, the receipts of the former being £35 less than in the previous year, whilst the Highway Department has exceeded its estimate by £1,372. £797 of this is accounted for by the decision of the committee to substitute Jarrah wood for the ordinary wood blocks,by an unsanctioned sum expended on paving in Crossley-street, and by extra purchase of stock. The estimated amount to be transferred, last year, from

div.head: GAS DEPARTMENT
div.p: THE GAS DEPARTMENT

in relief of the rates was £9,650. The amount actually received was £ll.lBl 19s. Bd., an excess of £4,532. The receipt of this sum largely accounts for the balance in the bank already alluded to of £2,786, and is the main factor in the reduction of the improvement rate. There was in last year's estimates, a sum of £1,400 which we expected to receive for a re-sale of certain property. This has, however, not yet been offered, and the amount has been inserted as a prospective receipt in the new estimate. And now to come to

THE NET EFFECT 'UPON THE RATES. The total amount requlied for the borough rate is £39,351, as against £35,580 last year, an increase of £3,771. 'he principal reason for this increase is that the education authority require £1,939 more that last year, and that we have to meet the adverse balance at the bank of £1,120. It is very gratifying to find that the overseers have already decided that they can meet this extra call without increasing the poor rate (which at present amounts to 4s. 4d.), thanks mainly to a con- siderable increase in the ratable value last year, and to the natural increment of the rates for the year which is now commencing. The difference they are safely able to take from their working balance. The total amount required for the improvement rite is £26,825, as against £27,799, a reduction of £974. I need not go into parti- culars as to how this reduction arises, but, coupled with the natural increment of the rate, and the fact that the areas which were subject to differential rating are now beginning to pay much larger amounts,it has enabled the Finance Committee to have the felicity of recommending a reduction on the improvement rate of twopence in the 2. The amount required for general sewers rate purposes is £1,205, as against £1,727 last year. This is due to the balance in the bank, and it enables the committee to recommend a reduction for the current year, under this head also, of twopence, making a current rate Of two- pence in the £, and a total present call of 7s. in the £. The rates have, therefore, shown a steady and continuous decrease from 7s. lOd. in 1904-5, to 7s. 81 in 1905-6, 7s. 4d. in 1906-7, and 7s. in 1907-8. I should like, at this point, to say that this highly satisfactory result is largely due to the energy and tact of our officials, to whom it is impossible to pay too high a compliment. The ratepayers themselves are also entitled to a hearty word of praise. The

ARREARS ARE QUITE ASTONISHINGLY SMALL. The total sure collected during the year, including water (the gas accounts are still unfortunately collected by a separate department) amounts to something like a hundred thousand pounds, and the total uncollected and irrecoverable items are considerably less than £lOO. I bad hoped to have had the pleasure of springing the welcome news of this further very substantial reduction upon you to-night, and putting you till in a state of high good humour, • but man proposes and newspaper editors dispose, and, although committees may pledge themselves to secrecy good tidings seem to fly apace. But I may, perhaps, be permitted to point out to you that, although we have been able to effect another reduction of fourpence in the 2, and to bring our total rates down to seven shillings, this does not by any means represent the whole of our internal stock-in- trade of satisfaction, for there are several other import- ant circumstances which I wish you all to bear in mind. In the first place, we are able to make the reduction in spite of the fact that the call for educational purposes has increased by nearly 2d. in the ; and, in the second place, it is concurrent with a reduction of 2d. per 1,090 cubic feet in the amount we charge for gas, which is egaivalent to another 21d. in the 2 upon the rates, so that, assuming the education rate to have remained stationary, and the Gas Committee to have continued to charge the old price, our total present reduction would have amounted to over eightpence in the 2. Ido not propose to enlarge upon the Education Estimates, Mr. Jolley went into them so fully and so lucidly before the Education Committee, and I do not wish to trespass on your time too long. Bat it is well to always bear in mind that we have

STAVED OFF A SCHOOL BOARD, and so kept down the rates for many years; that we have naturally a lot of leeway to make up ; and that, in spite of all this, our cost per child is only 7s. 4d. per head, the lowest save two of all the county boroughs in the country. Similar remarks apply to our rate for poor-law purposes, but it is not within my province to say anything under that head to-night. Vhe automatic rises in the teachers' salaries will, in due time, find their level (and it is to these that the increase in the amount required by the Education Committee is mainly due), whilst it must not be forgotten that we have lately added to our educational accommodation two big new departments. But nobody who has seen the Bearnont Schools can say that the money has not been well and wisely spent, and. whilst we wish to exercise due care and guard against extravagance, I defy any thoughtful and intelligent man to point to any better return for our municipal outlay than that which we expect to get in healthy 'limbs, and active minds, and strong and good and useful citizens. And now I wish, if possible, to stop the LAMENTATIONS OF THE LOCAL JEREMIAHS

by a few comparisons. For the ten years ended March 1867, the ideal rates amounted to an average of 54. 10,1 in the 2. Por the ten years eniing Vfarch, 1877 ss. 10d. ; ditto 1887, ss. B.?d. ; ditto, 1897, ss. 9,1. ; and for the six years ended March, 1903, 6s. 2d. After this, the Education Act becomes ai.disturbing factor and tne average rises to about 7s. 61d. The present charge for education is about is. sd. in the 2, of which a little over a Id. was charged, under the old arrangements, by the School Attendance Committee. This leaves an additional net charge for the current year of say is. which, deducted from the current rate of 7s. would bring the current rates down to ss. Bd. in the 2, a sum considerably below the average for the last 50 years. I may add that the highest rates, including education, in the 69 county boroughs of this country last year were paid in West Ham, and amounted to not less than 10s: 4d. in the 2, and that the average for the 69 was 75. Bd. in the 2. It is true that our rates for a time increased, but those who criticize them most have never given us credit for what we have got for them.

IMPROVEMENTS IN THE TOWN. Time will not permit me to more than allude to a few of the main items. We have widened Bridge-street at a total cost of something like £121,000, and turned one- half of Sankey-street into a boulevard. We have also widened Wilderspool-causeway, and large portions of the Knutsford, Manchester, and Liverpool-roads, as well RR part of Padgate-lane. We have acquired numerous blocks of property in various parts of the town in readiness for other necessary street improvements. We

div.head: ECONOMISTS
div.p: THE ECONOMISTS

were wise, perhaps, in putting on the brake, I hope with all my heart, in face of such results as I have shown, they will not seek to stop the coach. Much as we have done already, there is vastly more to do if Warrington is really to rise to all the height of its great oppor- tunity. Increasingly from year to year the public begin to look to the municipalities for life's amenities, if not, indeed, for many of its daily needs. Lord Avebury is a modern Mrs. Partington, and you cannot stop the broad Atlantic with a mop. (Laughter). The men who have so noisily taken up their parable against municipal trading in the sense in which I speak are like those foolish courtiers of King Canute who placed him on his throne beside the sea and Canute, him to tell the advancing tide that it was not to advance any further, but Canute got his feet wet, and the tide, I understand, flowed calmly on. (Laughter.) And so it is impossible to set an arbitrary limit to the progress of municipal enterprise, and what I want you all to do is to forget your differences and work together as one man and not to check this tide, but to direct it into proper channels; not to shut your ears to schemes which may be needful to promote the welfare of the town, but see, as Coun- cillor Pemberton says, that you get value for your money; to apply the brake when necessary; but to move steadily forward towards the goal—a Warrington, as I described it when I came before the electors first twelve years ago, "big, busy, and beautiful "—and to always recollect that, as you do not gauge a man's posi- tion by what he owes so much as by what he has, so you , should not judge a borough by its debt, but by the , excess of its assets over its liabilities; that probably ,no town in Lancashire has progressed so much as War- rington within so short a time; that our rates are steadily decreasing and are much below the average ; that our municipal enterprises are more productive than those of any other town in England save Carlisle; and that, if we wound up to-morrow, we could pay, say, 265. Bd. in the 2. (Applanse.)

div.head: RATES.
div.p: THE RATES.

The following resolutions were passed :- 1. That the Council hereby estimate the amount of .£39,351 7s. 11d, will in addition to the borough fund be required and sufficient for the purposes to which the borough fund is applicable,under the Municipal Cor- porations Act. 1882, or otherwise by law, for the year to end 31st March, 1908. 2. That the Council do hereby order a borough rate to be made in pursuance of the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, in order to raise the said amount.

_ 3. That the overseers of the township of Warrington be and they are hereby ordered to pay to the treasurer of the borough, by instalments, and on or before such dates no may ti i (Med by rinanna arta Tacitat. mittee, the contribution of the sum of £39,351 7s. 11d. out of the poor rate made or to be made for the said township of Warrington, as provided by the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882. 4. That the estimate for an improvement rate as recommended by the Finance and Estate Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance and Estate Committee to make an improvement rate accordingly at two shillings and sixpence in the pound, to be collected by two half-yearly instalments, and he anthorized to affix the Common Seal of the Corporation. 5. That the estimate of the general sewers rate as recommended by the Finance and Estate Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance and Estate Committee do make a general sewers rate accordingly at twopence in the pound, to be collected by Om half-yearly instal- ments, and be authorized to affix the Common Seal of the Corporation thereto. A WORD TO PROPERTY OWNERS.

Councillor STorr said they were all gratified the rates bad gone down during the last four years by 10d. in the Z. Some years ago thousands of rents of work- ing class houses were increased 3d. per week and some more than that. Seeing that property owners had been relieved to the extent of 10d. he hoped they would be as anxious to make some concession to the working class tenants as they were to put on the extra 3d. Instead of the rates being reduced so much he thought it would be better if they spent some of the money in erecting baths in connection with the Beamont School and the one to be built at Latchford. The Education Committee made a mistake in not asking the Council to expend money in that direction, and he hoped they would not attempt to build another public school with- out providing baths. THANKING ALDERMAN BENNETT. "A RADICAL SPEECH."

Councillor EVANS said it was with very great pleasure he proposed that the best thanks of the Council be given to Alderman Bennett for his able Budget speech. He did not know that he had ever listened to one with greater pleasure, and whilst he had no desire to flatter him he was sincere in the expnaseion he had just used. He had not only delivered a good speech, but had intro- duced some humour, and had shown the public the position of the town in a broader way than he had ever heard in a Budget speech. May had seen not only that the Council were accomplishing desirable objects, but what their position was so far as their indebtedness was concerned. These were very important points. (Hear, hear.) Councillor PEMBERTON seconded, and said he hoped to be able te have the pleasure of welcoming a similar reduction of the rates next year. There was no doubt that if Warrington was to prosper more than it had done in the past there must be these reductioes in the rates. The fact of having lower rates and plenty of facilities for manufacturers was bound to draw trade to Warrington. Then the whole of the inhabitants prospered, and they would he able to use to the best advantage some of the large municipal undertakings that had cost so much money. He could not agree with all Alderman Bennett had said in regard to the return for their money. He thought,considering the enormous capital they had invested, and the fact that they were not like similar undertakings conducted by private owners, but were municipalities, and had, therefore, a monopoly, that the return ought to be very handsome. He did not believe in the beautiful dream that Alder- man Bennett had referred to in times gone by—not that night—when they would have no rates to pay at all. (Laughter). The Ma. Yon : It is coming. (Renewed laughter.) Councillor PEMBERTON, continuing, said he did not quite agree that they had an asset and a capital value as Aldermen Bennett had put it. There were some things of no value ; they were only a sentimental value. It was time the Council put a check on extravagant expenditure, while he admitted it was essential they should spend on things which were necessary for the welfare of the town. It might he necessary to spend £1,000,000. It was not the amount of money but whether they got value for it. They could throw away as small a sum as £3OO as well as they could he wasteful in spending £3,000. If the Council would only go on as they had been going on for the past three. years, Warrington, owing to its intern( position, in Point of prosperity would be second to no town in England. (Hear, hear.) They had eight or nine rail- ways and practically the ocean at their door and two barge canals, in fact, they had everything a manufacturer required. Alderman FORST-14.W said the Budget speech had been a very aide and exhaustive one: and he should not be surprised if some day they found Alderman Bennett occupying the position of Chancellor of the Exchequer, (Laughter.) Conneillor HAWTHORN said the Alderman had, in his opinion, given the Council a very Radical speech. (Laughter.) The sentiments he had given expression to would come as quite a shock to the municipal reformers in London, and would startle the members of his own party. He (the speaker) agreed with the Alderman's advanced views on municipalization, and the Council was greatly indebted to him for the lead he had given in the matter.

The NIAXOn. in putting the resolntion to the meeting, said he also wished to congratulate the Alderman upon the pleasing and n,ble speech he had made. It WM certainly very gratifying to (Ind a reduction in the rates

of 4s. in the 2. He was grateful to the Council for getting through such a long and difficult agenda so expeditiously. The motion was agreed to with hearty applause. Alderman BENNETT, in replying, said he had honestly tried to place the broad general facts before the Council as clearly as he could, and to give a real idea of the present financial condition of the town. They had all felt that there was some little danger of going too fast and that it was to some extent necessary to put the brake,on. At the same time he had also felt that what- ever they did they must go ahead if they wished the town to achieve the possibilities which had been sketched by Councillor Pembertou. (Hear, hear.) It was gratifying to find that the results of their united efforts—and he gave credit to no one section of the Cotincil—was so satisfactory. They had all honestly done their best to get the town into a thoroughly sound financial position and to couple real satisfactory progress with the efficiency which was necessary to permanent progress. The result had worked out more satisfactorily than he had imagined possible. He hoped they would proceed in that policy and go slowly and cautiously, but always be moving, and try to achieve something better than they had achieved in the past. There was no reason why Warrington should not be able to attract to its borders many large industries, land develop into a beautiful, large, important, and prosperous commercial town. (Applause). In reply to Councillor Hawthorn, he wished to state that they must not think that he, a Conservative,would allow the other I side to have the credit of all the • intelligence. I (Laughter). He was not speaking in a political senstNit was only good nature, bat there were many Conserva- tives of great capacity, and who possessed the faculty of seeing things as they were, and adapting themselves to the conditions of the present day. If Councillor Hawthorn thought the Conservatism with which he (Alderman Bennett) was associated was identified with retrograde policies he was very much mistaken. • (Applause).

div.head: KEEP IT DAR K.
div.p: KEEP IT DAR K.
New Rendering of an 91d Song.

I hear some strange news as I travel along, Keep it dark; At this time of year something always goes wrong, Keep it dark; We need not, of course, believe all that we're told, Truth and Error are mixed, same as silver and gold, So think what you like of the tales I unfold,
But keep it dark. We are wanting, I hear, a new Chief for the bobbies Keep it dark; Let us get one, they say, without too many hobbies,
Keep'it dark. Is it true, do you think, that some7.P.'s may booze, iltay go home at all hours of the night as they choose. That bobbies can't see when they're having a snooze: Keep it dark.
We've just been considering the Workhouse affair,
Keep it dark; It's getting so grand that I want to live there, _
Keep it dark. There are some Poor Law Guardians we call Jolly Spenders, And some-are described as our Guardian Pretender- ; I vote for Reformers and all Poor Law Menders;
Keep it dark. The worst change in " Guardians "we've had, if its true,.
Keep it dark, Is mixing the Sankey Street " Neutral" with blue;
Keep it dark. They say that John Barleycorn's got a bfg share ; That it's either a Green-Hall or Parr-Hall affair. Of brewers,and brewers of mischief beware • Keep it 'dark.
Ananias of old kept back part of the. price;

He kept it dark-. To keep part of the land is a modern device; Keep it dark. A petition was signed, were the facts all revealed? Many ratepayers thought they were buying a field; If the purchase is made, are the terms still concealed? They keep it dark. I hear that C. B. is considering a plan, _ _ _
_ - Keep it dark ; To deal with the Suffragists, cunning old man, _
, _ . He 'keeps it dark. They have to call meetings in every place, To decide which of them has the prettiest face ; If any survive, they can then state their case,
Keep it dark. , The Ritualists really are going too far,

Keep it dark; We shall soon be quite puzzled to know where we ares Keep it dark. Their books of confession all Englishmen shock, Against all such parsons or doors we should lock; Or we'll have to confess when we wind up the clock, A
Or, keep it dark. I've let you off easily just for a treat„
Keep it dark And I'll tell you some "stiff uns " the next time we' meet,
Keep it dark. If yon don't quite agree with the things that I say, With my rhymes on the times in my topical way, T can easily alter them some other day, But, keep it dark. MEP HISTO

div.head: SEQUEL TO A FARM FATALITY. ---- Unsuccessful Claim for Compensation.
div.p: SEQUEL TO A FARM FATALITY. ---- Unsuccessful Claim for Compensation.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Deputy-Judge Strachan, K.C., George Holt, labourer, Booth's Hill, Lymm. claimed under the Work' men's Compensation Act, £3OO for the loss of his son, Charles Holt (36) who was killed by falling under threshing machine at Booth's Farm, Lymm, on October 11th, 1906. The respondents were Messrs. Edward Massa and Arthur Massey. Booth's Farm. Cherry-lane, Lymni. farmers, and the Warrington and District Threshing Co., Lythgoe's-lane, Warrington.—Mr. Dockray (Messrs. Bindlogg and Doolcray), of Manchester. appeared fa George Holt: Mr. Arthur Browne for the respondent Massey. and Mr. Cuthbart Smith (instructed by Mr, T. S. Steel) for the District Threshing Co. Mr. Dockray said that on October 11th deceased wag engaged in moving a thrashing machine when the ground on which it was standing gave way and he wao fatally injured. Applicant and his wife were partially dependent on the deceased's earnings. The difficulty appbared to be as to who was the employer Qf the deceased, but on the facts of the case he thought he was employed by the Threshing Company. The evidence he should call was to the effect that deceased was engaged by man named Edward Massey, but he was not Edward Massey the respondent but the man in charge of the eneine.

His Honour: Deceased was not an ordinary farra labourer en gaged in agriculture? Mr. Dockray : The practice appears to he that when a threshing machine goes to a farm extra hands follow it. Continuing he said that when the accident happened deceased was assisting to get the machine ready to be moved away. At the time Holt was killed he had not been paid any wages. The follow- in morning the applicant went to the farm and wag paid by one of the Masdey's 2s. 6d.—the wages of the deceased. Deceased was a single man and when in full work had earned 18s. a week. The father was a farni labourer, 62 years ace, in casual employment. Samuel Daniels. farm labour' Lymm, who was work- ing with deceased, described the accident. Deceased was working on the top of the tank when it gave waY and he was crushed under the machine. Arthur Massey, driver of the machine, engaged deceased, but witness was engaged by the farmer. In answer to Mr. Browne, witness said it wasythe custom for men to follow the threshing machine from farm to farm, and whoever they were engaged by they were subject to the orders of the driver. When the corn had been threshed the farmers had nothing to do with the machine.
13y Mr. Cuthbert Smith: The driver of the engine did not toll them to move the mess. The farmer always enraged the men who followed the machine and paid them.

Hannah Holt, mother of the deceesed, spoke as to the partial dependence of her husband and herself upon deceased's earnings. She had received £2 from the Threshing Company and 7s. 6d. from Masses's towards the foneral expenses. By nr. Cuthbert Smith: She always understood ' that men who did deceased's work where employed by the farmer. _ _
_ G.nrle Holt, the.anplicant, Mao gave evidence.

. , Mr. Brown submitted that he had no case to answer ns it was sworn by the witness Daniels that deceased was engszed by the driver of the threshing machine. His Honour: You have certainly a case to answer es it stsnds at present. The evidence is that the farmer has certain men on the farm. When the engine comes with the driver and two other men as being the engineer's department, whatever other men are required the farmer selects. It may he that he delegates the duty to the driver, but he pays the men's wages. Mr. Cuthh4rt Smith: I say I have no case to answer on that evidence, and if there is a case for Mr. Browne to answer, there cannot be a case for me. His Honour: That does not follow. Mr. Cuthbert Smith : I venture to say it does in this 'asse. The only Possible statement that sounds like evidence acainst me is that Bolt was engaged by the ent,ina Arivcr. There is no evidence that he was enzaged hT the Comnany, and unless he was, I am not liable under the Act. Hiq Honour held that the Threshing Company were not liable and discharged them from the case. With rseard to costa he had no alternative but to allow theta but he thought Mr. Dockray might make a fair appeal to the company. Mr. Browne said that no one in responsibility gave the men orders to move the machine. Deceased's day'g work was over as far as the farmers were concerned, On the snur nf the moment the men began to move the nress and through some unexplained cause the accident hannened. His Honour held that the deceased was not in the employ of the farmer when the accident happened and gave judgment for the respondents with costs.

TO COMMENCE TTIE " EXAMINER," APRIL 27Til. • BREATHLESS EXCITEMENT! THRILLING SENSATION!! THE EXPLOITS OF THE ONE-EYED MAN. EIGHT NARRATIVES BY EDWARD TOWLER In which are related the amazing experienoes of a human fiend who for a brief period terrorised England. This audacious scoundrel defied the police, and the smartest detectives of England and America were unable to lay him by the heels. He robbed a big bank in broad daylight, captured a specie van on our greatest railway, and kidnapped a multi-millionaire. Priceless pictures and jesvels worth a king's ransom were among the booty secured by the fearless gang of outlaws led by the One-Eyed Man. A veritable Napoleon of crime, this twentieth century terror undertook to steal the signal books from a British warship, and actually succeeded ! It is AN ASTOUNDING RECORD and will be eagerly read. In many respects the series is unique. The tales are told without any attempt at melodramatic embellishment, in a plain, straightforward way which makes them intensely realistic. They grip as power- fully as a strong serial, and anyone who reads the first story will want to follow the adven- tures of the One-Eyed Man to the end. LOOK OUT FOR "THE ONE-EYED MAN." A rare metal which has attracted universal attention during the last two years, while before it was scarcely known outside of some scientific laboratories, is tantalum, so named by its discoverer, Ekelberg, on account of the tantalizing difficulties experienced in extracting the metal from its ores. Only two years ago was it found out by German scientists that what the discoverer thought to be tantalum was an alloy of it and a carbide, and more tantalizing efforts were necessary to produce this metal in its perfectly pure state ; but this succeEs once being reached, the metal immediately became of such importance that it is now revolutionising at least one large industry, that of the rtanufacture of incandescent lamps for electric lights. Although it has been tried to use tantalum as a steel-hardening agent, the mechanical difficulties in alloying tantalum with steel have been so great that we shall probably see other applications come into promi- nence first. Tantalum is one of the hardest substances known and its use for scientific instruments, where price stands always second to accuracy and durability, will doubtless be developed much sooner, inasmuch as tantalum also resists the corrosive influence of acids and alkalide solutions to a very remarkable degree. One of the most striking experiments to demonstrate the hardness of tantalum was, that for the purpose of boring a hole through a sheet of pure tantalum metal, a diamond drill-bore was used, revolving incessantly for three days and making 5,000 ravolutions per minute,and the result was a depression of less than one-hundredth of an inch in the metal, but an entirely dull and smooth diamond.—E. Schaaf-Regelman, in "The Engineering Magazine" for April. ----- .
